📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Uno Platform 7.0 Adds WebGPU Backend, Apple TV and Reactor Support, and Retires Native Rendering.

Nov 16, 2026 3 min read.

The Uno Platform team released Uno Platform 7.0, which unifies rendering on SkiaSharp 4 with an experimental WebGPU backend, adds Apple TV as a target platform and supports .NET 11 from day zero. The release also brings third-party .NET MAUI controls and Microsoft.UI.Reactor library to every target, and removes native rendering and Mac Catalyst.

Recent findings suggest that uno Platform is an open-source framework for building .NET applications with C# and WinUI XAML for Windows, Android, iOS, macOS, Linux and WebAssembly. The team describes 7.0 as its largest release, with 5,219 commits and 704 closed issues since 6.7. According to the team’s benchmarks, 7.0 is about 2x faster at the median and 5x smaller than 6.7, with some operations, such as brush creation, up to 38x faster. These figures come from the vendor and the workloads were not published in detail.

All targets now render through one pluggable pipeline. SkiaSharp 4 is the default, and Uno Platform is a co-maintainer of the library alongside the .NET team at Microsoft. On Android, Windows and Linux, Skia now renders through Vulkan by default. The WebGPU backend, available on all desktop, mobile and WebAssembly targets, is enabled by adding WebGpu to UnoFeatures and registering the backend on the host builder. It uses wgpu-native outside the browser and the browser’s own WebGPU support on WebAssembly. The team measured up to a 50% frame-rate improvement depending on the scene, and claims a WebGPU-only app drops about 6 MB of uncompressed native code from WebAssembly builds. A fresh WebGpuCanvasElement lets applications issue their own WebGPU commands inside the UI.

In a recent development, through .NET MAUI Embedding, controls from vendors such as Syncfusion, Telerik, Infragistics, DevExpress and Esri previously ran only on iOS, Android, macOS and Windows. They now work on every Uno Platform target, including the web and Linux. In the other direction, existing .NET MAUI apps can reach the browser and Linux through Uno Platform’s .NET MAUI handlers.

Industry observers note that microsoft.UI.Reactor, Microsoft’s declarative C# framework for WinUI with hooks such as UseState and no XAML, now runs on desktop, browser, Android and iOS. It is enabled with the Reactor UnoFeature, is in preview, and can coexist with existing XAML pages in the same visual tree. Apple TV support is added through the net10.0-tvos target framework, targets tvOS 15 and later, renders through Metal and uses the Siri Remote for focus navigation. .NET 11 is supported on every head, for example through dotnet new unoapp -tfm net11.0, while .NET 10 remains the long-term support option.

RichTextBlock and RichEditBox are now available on every platform, closing an problem opened in 2018. WinUI alignment continues with ItemsRepeater and ItemsView ported from current WinUI sources, LinedFlowLayout, the TitleBar control, multiple windows on iPad and Lottie rendering through Composition. Smaller additions include built-in input validation through INotifyDataErrorInfo, TalkBack, VoiceOver and AT-SPI screen-reader support, and the uno-devserver app command for launching and inspecting running apps from scripts and CI.

It has been revealed that most apps upgrade by changing the Uno.Sdk version in global.json, following the migration guide. The team released Uno Platform Studio 3.3 alongside it.

Industry observers note that the release follows Uno Platform 6.7 in September, which added Android TV, Android Auto and Wear OS targets, semantic styles shared by the Material and Simple themes, and damage-region repainting on Skia renderers. It also removed the WPF targets.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • "Infoblox is investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor,” a company spokesperson confirmed to The Register.
  • According to sources, the compromised third-party data migration vendor had trusted access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, and the intruders used this vendor’s accounts and access to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Networking and security firm Infoblox is investigating a third-party breach that allowed crims to access sensitive customer and staff data.

"Infoblox is investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor,” a company spokesperson confirmed to The Register.

According to sources, the compromised third-party data migration vendor had trusted access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, and the intruders used this vendor’s accounts and access to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint.

This data included configuration information related to some customer's NIOS (Network Identity Operating System) deployments. These are saved snapshots of customers’ network data, such as DNS, DHCP configurations, Grid databases, and reporting logs, that can be used to fully recover the appliance or grid in case of a system failure or faulty upgrade.

It has been revealed that the intruders also stole employee data during the break-in. According to an email CEO Scott Harrell sent to employees, which The Register has seen, compromised employee details include financial information such as direct deposit details, contact info, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents.

Upon discovering the breach, Infoblox “immediately activated” its incident response procedures, and took steps to contain the incident, including hiring outside cybersecurity experts, the spokesperson mentioned.

“We have sent notifications about this security event and are providing support and guidance as appropriate,” the Infoblox spokesperson told us. “Based on our investigation to date, we have no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Our priority is to fully investigate and resolve this matter.".

Affected staff received a $100 "spot bonus" to buy password management services, and were warned to be "especially alert for phishing, vishing, fraud, or other suspicious communications." Infoblox also gave employees and their dependents free credit monitoring and identity protection for two years.

Infoblox declined to answer our more detailed questions about the compromise, including the type of data exposed, and how many employees and customers might be affected.

The Register will upgrade this story as we learn more about the breach.®.

  • The decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound.
  • Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B. These add a speculative decoding path that trades a minimal memory increase for a large decoding speedup without changing output quality:.

The decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound. Most latency comes from streaming weights from DRAM into SRAM, not from intense computation. Speculative decoding addresses this by using a lightweight draft model to produce candidate tokens, then having the target model verify them all in a single forward pass, sharing the cost of loading the weights across all tokens we verify.

Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:.

It has been revealed that we follow the DSpark recipe with a larger and more diverse data mix covering SFT, chat, code, and function-calling data. Based on our ablations, the first versions of the draft models are simplified attention-only draft models, with 5 layers and a block of 9. For each draft model, we ran 15 epochs on the entire dataset and selected the epoch with the highest acceptance rate rather than the lowest loss.

The resulting draft models are relatively small, with each around ~300M parameters.

Industry observers note that under greedy decoding, a draft token is only accepted if it matches the target model’s distribution. On rejection, the target model's own token takes its place. The emitted sequence is therefore identical to baseline greedy by construction, so benchmark accuracy (pass@1 or exact match) is unchanged.

Our DSpark draft models for LFM2.5 ship with day-one support for llama.cpp (implementation builds on top of the official codebase, which we run with experimental metal kernels) and **SGLang (**implementation builds on the official SGLang implementation of DSpark).

We measure on-device throughput with llama.cpp and Metal on an M4 Max MacBook Pro using FP16 GGUF weights and up to 256 output tokens. We measure GPU throughput with SGLang on a single H100 80 GB in BF16. Both configurations use a DSpark block size of 9, a batch size of 1, and a temperature of 0. We evaluate them on five benchmark datasets.

All three drafter models deliver noticeable throughput improvements on both the large-scale accelerator (H100) and the edge deployment (M4 Max MacBook).

For LFM2.5-2.6B, speedup on the MacBook is especially noticeable, as it pushes the interactivity level a user can enjoy far beyond the throughput offered by most proprietary cloud models (around ~140 tok/s, depending on the dataset).

Across various multi-tool scenarios, DSpark reduces the latency by 57% on average for LFM2.5-2.6B.

For LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, we see much more variance in dataset acceptance rates, so speedup varies by as much as 52% depending on the underlying text distribution.

Sources indicate that for LFM2.5-8B-A1B, the acceptance rate increases compared to two dense models, yet on-device we get only an 18% improvement on average. This gap is due to the current MoE implementation in llama.cpp's Metal backend, and to the fact that verifying k tokens activates more experts and thus more weight traffic than a single decode step.

In a recent development, running the DSpark draft models with SGLang requires an SGLang build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #31041). Launch the target with the draft attached:.

In a recent development, then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:30000/v1. The block size is read from the draft's config.json; the baseline is the same command without the three --speculative-* flags.

Running them with llama.cpp requires the respective llama.cpp build (PR#27383).

Sources indicate that the block size is read from the sidecar metadata (n-max is clamped to it). Speculative decoding is exact: the target verifies every proposed token, so greedy output equals the target alone; per-response timings report draft_n / draft_n_accepted.

The DSpark draft model checkpoints are available on Hugging Face as Safetensors and in GGUF format:.

We can’t wait to see what you build.

California sues OpenAI for misleading public about AI safety

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A-G cites Hugging Face incident as example of why industry must be accountable.
  • California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI under the state's unfair competition and public nuisance laws, for allegedly misleading and endangering the public by deploying unsafe AI models.
  • The lawsuit [PDF], filed in California Superior Court, follows the compromise of Hugging Face's infrastructure and other cyber incidents OpenAI's experimental models caused when taking autonomous actions without authorization or supervision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A-G cites Hugging Face incident as example of why industry must be accountable.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI under the state's unfair competition and public nuisance laws, for allegedly misleading and endangering the public by deploying unsafe AI models.

The lawsuit [PDF], filed in California Superior Court, follows the compromise of Hugging Face's infrastructure and other cyber incidents OpenAI's experimental models caused when taking autonomous actions without authorization or supervision.

"While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents," noted Attorney General Bonta.

At a press conference, Bonta added: "OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public.".

Recent findings suggest that the legal salvo comes after Bonta in September sent OpenAI a letter seeking information about these agentic attacks. According to the complaint, "OpenAI failed to substantially comply" with the investigatory subpoena.

In August, 15 states led by Iowa – and excluding California – issued a joint demand for OpenAI to provide information about how its models hacked Hugging Face.

OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.

Bonta's office previously joined with Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings to urge OpenAI to do more for children's safety in light of reports that its models produced sexually inappropriate output. California did not, however, join the eight states that sued OpenAI in October over alleged misrepresentations about child safety. Florida and Texas have also made child safety claims.

Child safety plays well politically; California appears to be the first state to demand more accountability toward the general public.

Bonta's lawsuit, in a state that has largely accommodated the AI industry for the sake of economic benefits and political contributions, suggests that California officials may be more willing to bite the hand that feeds.

The many Democratic victories in the US midterm elections may also be a factor, as pundits feel voters swung to give lawmakers license to regulate the unpopular AI industry.

At his press conference, Bonta made sure to convey that he wants accountability without smothering the AI industry in costly regulation.

Industry observers note that "Let me be clear," he said. "I believe in the technological and economic power of AI. If we're able to address these very high stakes safety concerns, AI could lead to some of the most incredible improvements in the history of humankind.".

Sources indicate that AI is yet to deliver those incredible improvements. It has delivered deepfakes, huge quantities of cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and the permissionless resale of past intellectual labor, plus high energy and RAM prices. As well as some productivity gains in certain areas like coding, albeit at an unknown cost to future job markets.

But as AI boosters insist, miracle drugs and endless vacations aren't far off … perhaps along with existential crises.

Katharine Trendacosta, director of policy and advocacy at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told The Register in an email that the EFF is glad to see state officials taking action against AI companies taking unreasonable risks with public safety.

"Several recent cybersecurity incidents at AI labs could have been prevented or substantially mitigated by adhering to longstanding cybersecurity best practices, such as proper sandboxing, monitoring, and logging," stated Trendacosta.

"AI agents can be useful tools when deployed appropriately, with adequate safeguards designed to mitigate the risks. Companies should carefully consider the risks of every use case, including the consequences, reversibility, and sensitivity of any action an agent is used for." ®.

#23237. Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

📅 21 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1778 w)

Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

📅 21 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels.
  • It has been revealed that one reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice.
  • Recent findings suggest that however, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

It has been revealed that one reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

Recent findings suggest that however, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Sources indicate that our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

Sources indicate that in some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was noted, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

It has been revealed that voxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio indicates, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

It has been revealed that for example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a new parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

The reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually states the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Voice clone of the same speaker.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff.

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

The results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

To build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:.

2011 draft budget (masked numbers).

Recent findings suggest that recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11.

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11.

According to recent reports, within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

According to recent reports, our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister.".

It has been revealed that multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

In a recent development, to test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

In a recent development, other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

For people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Industry observers note that our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to upcoming audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

Quality IMAP, Part 1: Your Mailbox Is A Database

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deuxfleurs

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During the past year, we have significantly improved the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation.
  • According to recent reports, aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network problems and hardware failures.
  • Industry observers note that implementing an IMAP server is not easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the past year, we have significantly improved the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation. This is the first part in a series of blog posts elaborating on why implementing IMAP correctly is not so easy, and the set of techniques we have been using to make our IMAP code as high-quality as we can. In this first part, we focus on one challenging aspect of IMAP: fine-grained retrieval and querying of emails.

According to recent reports, aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network problems and hardware failures. It is built on top of Garage and shares the same philosophy. Aerogramme is AI-free: we do not wish to use unethical technology and prefer to spend effort on careful craftmanship and community-building.

Industry observers note that implementing an IMAP server is not easy. Partly because IMAP is an old protocol, with a good number of extensions that has accumulated quite a bit of complexity over time. On top of that IMAP provides - for good reasons - two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement: fine-grained retrieval and querying of email contents and concurrent multi-client multi-session access to mailboxes.

This is the first part in a series of posts discussing how we have been approaching IMAP access. In the past year, we have been refining Aerogramme's IMAP implementation to be "more correct", in a context where "correctness" is unfortunately not always well specified: IMAP and email are defined in documents that are often vague, and furthermore, real-world implementations do not always follow specifications.

Today, we'll walk you though our work on the correctness and reliability of Aerogramme for retrieving and querying emails, and explain why your mailbox is, in fact, a database...

This work was funded by NLNet under the "Aerogramme 1.0" grant, and could not have been possible without their support.

Feel free to join the Aerogramme matrix channel for updates or if you just want to chat!

One challenge of the IMAP specification is the rich feature-set it provides for retrieving mailbox and email contents. We may sometimes think of a mailbox as a directory containing plain email files; however, from the point of view of an IMAP server (or client), a mailbox is closer to a database, accessed using a dedicated query language.

It has been revealed that for instance, mobile clients, which have slower and unreliable connectivity, benefit from fine-grained querying of a mailbox contents. User experience is much better if an email client can selectively fetch the subject of upcoming emails (to enhancement the list of emails in the mailbox) without having to first download all of their attachments or doing a sync of the entire mailbox.

To facilitate the mobile client use-case, IMAP specifies two key mechanisms for querying and (partial) retrieval of emails in a mailbox:.

Recent findings suggest that A direct consequence of these features is that an IMAP server actually needs to parse the emails, not just store them. It then needs to (correctly) interpret the (sometimes tricky) query language of SEARCH and FETCH, and internally support a data architecture that enable efficiently searching and querying over the emails.

Our implementation of SEARCH and FETCH is backed by the three following components:.

The logic for SEARCH and FETCH is implemented as an interpreter that takes already parsed emails and walks down their AST to evaluate IMAP-specific queries1. This separates email structure (email ASTs do not depend on IMAP concepts) from IMAP-specific business logic. This layer has been significantly reworked in the last months, fixing a good number of logic bugs and edge cases in our implementation of the SEARCH and FETCH IMAP specification.

Email parsing is done using the eml-codec companion library, that we also develop and maintain. The eml-codec library parses emails into a rich, structured AST while also giving access to raw input slices that correspond to relevant AST nodes; this is required for implementing FETCH. In the past year, eml-codec has evolved from an email parsing library with IMAP-specific quirks to a robust, well-tested, general-purpose email library with support for both parsing and printing of emails. You can read more about the library design choices in our work-in-progress design document.

Aerogramme's internal data architecture splits mailbox state, email metadata, and email contents. It is briefly described in Aerogramme's documentation. Mailbox state (emails IDs and flags) and email metadata (parsed headers, date, size) are stored in Aerogramme's metadata storage using Garage K2V, while email contents are stored in blob storage using Garage S3. This allows SEARCH to be efficient by only reading pre-computed information in metadata storage. At the moment there are no other significant optimizations for FETCH/SEARCH; the likely next step would be to add a full-text search engine.

These components are all quite non-trivial! Let's now talk about the strategies we've deployed to make them as correct as we could.

We ran our implementation of FETCH and SEARCH through ImapTest: a testing tool for IMAP servers maintained by the Dovecot developers. ImapTest was invaluable in surfacing issues with FETCH and SEARCH, but is equally useful to test all other aspects of IMAP.

According to recent reports, most relevant for FETCH and SEARCH was the test suite provided with ImapTest: a collection of hand-crafted test scenarios testing many subtle or "interesting" aspects of the IMAP specification. Each scenario consists of IMAP commands to send to the server, and a specification of the corresponding expected responses.

Running the ImapTest test suite found a small number of bugs in SEARCH, mostly in edge-cases of the specification. However, testing FETCH revealed that our initial implementation of the BODY[] subcommand was conceptually wrong in many cases! This subcommand of FETCH retrieves a sub-part of an email by following its structure, which we implement by walking down the email's AST. Our initial implementation was done by reading the IMAP specification and interpreting its sometimes vague wording as best as we could; only testing with ImapTest made us realize that our best-guess interpretation was wrong in many cases. More precisely: it did not match ImapTest's reading of the spec, which, in doubt, is what we prefer to follow!

ImapTest was also relatively pleasant to use to do manual "differential testing" for any remaining edge-cases: when we had any doubt, we could easily write additional scenarios and compare Aerogramme's output with Dovecot's; treating Dovecot as an oracle. After a few rounds of bugfixing, Aerogramme's implementation of FETCH and SEARCH is now in much better shape.

Recent findings suggest that the lesson we learned is that the IMAP specification can leave room for interpretation in surprising ways. In fact, to further illustrate this point, let's talk about one ImapTest scenario that we haven't "fixed" yet in Aerogramme because we just found it very confusing, and we are not sure what to do!

It has been revealed that he's a tricky case. SEARCH FROM returns the list of emails whose From header "contains" the given string. Now, what does "contains" mean here, exactly? When running SEARCH FROM foo@example.com on the two following headers, which ones should match?

Recent findings suggest that some additional context on email syntax is useful here: these two email addresses are equivalent. The local-part of the email (before the @) allows quoted strings, so "foo" can be used and simply denotes foo. Email syntax also allows comments in various places; they are written between parentheses. Comments have no formal meaning but are shown by email clients and can be useful; they are sometimes used by mailing-list software to indicate the name of the list. As an example SYMPA emits From headers of the form From: Alice (via Super Friends List) ).

At the moment, Aerogramme implements SEARCH FROM as plain substring search on the text representation of the header: here, the first header matches, but not the second. However, the ImapTest test suite says that both headers should match! So, what does the specification says?

The IMAP specification2 for SEARCH says:.

Hmm, so, what is this "envelope structure"? Reading further:.

So the FROM field of an email's "envelope structure" contains a structured representation of parsed email addresses. Regarding our two headers above, they are both represented in the envelope structure as:.

It has been revealed that what does it mean for this structured value to "contain" the string foo@example.com? Clearly none of the strings in the structure contain foo@example.com, so perhaps instead we should re-print the structure as an email address and do a substring search on that? However, there is not a unique way of printing a given email address, and the IMAP specification does not define any...

We are quite curious to know if IMAP experts have more to say on this point!

In the meantime, our bugfixes for FETCH and SEARCH have been shipped in Aerogramme 0.5.1 (see the release notes for more details), with the exception of two extra fixes shipped in Aerogramme 0.6.

FETCH and SEARCH operate on the parsed email ASTs produced by eml-codec. How do we ensure that we have correctly implemented all the subtleties of the email format in eml-codec, which is itself described in an old and tricky set of specifications? As often, the answer is: more testing.

According to recent reports, to ensure our implementation is correct, we performed fuzzer-guided Property-Based Testing (PBT) of the email parser and printer in eml-codec. Specifically, we tested the following "roundtrip" property:.

âfor an arbitrary email value in eml-codec's internal AST, printing it then parsing the printed output must yield an equivalent ASTâ.

In a recent development, the starting AST is generated by a fuzzer as a structured value using the Arbitrary trait; the cargo-fuzz tutorial calls this "Structure-Aware Fuzzing". A roundtrip in the other direction, i.e. "parse then print then test for string equality" would not generally hold, as there are many equivalent ways of printing the same email, for instance because of line folding...

While it may seem that any reasonable implementation would satisfy our roundtrip property, in practice, this methodology immediately surfaced a lot of bugs and edge cases.

The recurring theme was that the fuzzer would generate "exotic" AST values breaking the roundtrip property, for which we had to clarify:.

Industry observers note that in the first case, this fixed bugs or potential security issues for consumers of the parser (like Aerogramme) or printer. In the second case, it improved the definition of internal AST types, which is relevant when using eml-codec to programatically compose emails, not something we use in Aerogramme itself, but relevant for an experimental mailing-list server project in Deuxfleurs using the same library.

To illustrate the kind of issues that we are talking about here, let's look at an tricky example that was found using our fuzzing methodology.

It has been revealed that the "MIME Part Three" specification (RFC2047) specifies a way of using non-ASCII text in selected places of email headers. (Full support for UTF-8 in headers, which eml-codec also supports, was only introduced later.) Where allowed by the specification, ASCII text can be replaced by an "encoded word": an ASCII encoding of non-ASCII text using special syntax introduced by the specification.

As an example, the UTF-8 word aÃ©rogramme can be encoded as follows:.

More generally, a MIME encoded word has the following structure:.

When using the q encoding like above, most ASCII characters can be used directly in the encoded text, and other bytes must be encoded as = followed by their hexadecimal code.

Now, let us consider the following From header:.

Recent findings suggest that this looks like an encoded word followed by some extra junk; is this a valid From header? Perhaps surprisingly, there is no encoded word in this header, and it is a valid email address! The email address is =?utf-8?q? @ [?= X] (it is technically valid!), where the part after the '@' uses the uncommon "domain-literal" syntax.

Now, consider the following Subject header with the same byte representation:.

This time, the first part of the header is an encoded word, and the whole header tells us that the subject is the string @[ X]!

The explanation for this behavior follows from the specification (which is fairly clear on this aspect): the set of ASCII characters that can be used unescaped in depends on the context in which the encoded word appears.

In a recent development, encoded words can appear in From headers (for example From: =?utf-8?q?a=C3=A9rogramme?= is valid), but in that context they cannot use @ or [ unescaped, which is why the first example does not in fact contain a valid encoded word. In the context of a Subject header, the set of valid unescaped characters is broader and includes both @ and [, making =?utf-8?q?@[?= is a valid encoded word representing the string @[.

It has been revealed that to implement this behavior, we needed to correctly track the context in which we parse encoded words, "tokenize" them according to that context, and also track context sensitivity in our email AST and during printing. Getting every detail to align properly between parsing, our internal AST, and printing took us several attempts! In that process, our property-testing setup was extremely useful, as it could quickly come up with fresh convoluted examples like the one above that revealed bugs in edge cases of our code.

The lesson here is that email specifications can be quite complicated and tricky to implement, even when they are clear! And, in our experience, without automatic test generation (like our fuzzer setup), it is very hard to manually come up with examples that actually cover edge cases...

If you want to see more details, the bulk of our PBT/fuzzing work on eml-codec was done in eml-codec 0.3 and shipped in Aerogramme 0.4, with some additional improvements shipped in Aerogramme 0.6.

We tested eml-codec on collections of real-world emails (more than 100k emails) to evaluate and improve the recovery strategies of eml-codec's parser on invalid or broken syntax.

Recent findings suggest that many legitimate emails found in the real world are, indeed, incorrect with respect to email specifications. Often, the use of invalid or broken syntax is local (to specific headers, or parts of a header); in some cases, it is "only" a minor deviation from the specification.

The case of "message IDs" can be taken as an example. Emails can be given an identifier (specified using the Message-ID header) so that later emails can reference it (using the In-Reply-To and References headers). This is useful to display email "threads" in email clients, for example. The message ID syntax is also used to identify attachments with the Content-ID header.

Reading the specification, a message ID is of the form:.

and a list of message IDs as used by In-Reply-To and References separates message IDs with whitespace:.

The specification also documents that, for the list syntax, "obsolete" syntax (that we must support) can include extra text surrounding message IDs...

Now, what do we find in our sample of real-world emails?

-> Emitted by apple-mail, and invalid: no @!

-> Invalid: no angle brackets !

-> Valid: an instance of the "obsolete" syntax documented by the specification.

-> Commas are valid as part of the obsolete syntax, but the second message-id is malformed because of incorrect line folding (\n\t) in the middle of a word.

Recent findings suggest that the consequence is that eml-codec needs to be able to recover from broken syntax: on an email containing invalid syntax, it should be able to discard the broken parts and parse as much as it can from the rest of the email, instead of simply returning an error. It should also ideally be able to parse invalid but common deviations from the specifications in order to recover information instead of discarding them.

We first extended eml-codec with coarse-grained recovery strategies, such as discarding an entire header field if we couldn't parse it. This allowed us to quickly reach a state where the eml-codec parser is a total function: for any input bytes, it always returns an email AST representing an RFC-compliant email3, discarding any part of the input it does not understand.

Recent findings suggest that we then instrumented the parser to log each time it discards broken input when recovering, and ran the instrumented parser on the email that we collected. This gave us a lot of examples of legitimate emails with broken syntax. In each case, then, we manually looked at the piece of broken syntax, see if we could make some sense of it, and decide whether:.

This whole process was particularly interesting because it made us face the many subtleties of real-world emails (sometimes far from the "truth" of specifications); eml-codec is now much more robust operating on real-world emails!

Industry observers note that this methodology involves a lot of tradeoffs and judgment calls: there is a limit to the amount of parsing hacks that we can add in terms of code quality but also parsing ambiguity; and some classes of emails are more critical than others (e.g. we should not spend too much effort supporting spam emails). A strong design constraint of eml-codec is that, up to a few exceptions, we want its internal AST to only represent RFC-compliant emails, so we did not want to pollute it to include random broken syntax just for the sake of "recovering more". The whole process, in particular, helped us clarify the design of eml-codec as a library.

Recent findings suggest that for more details, you can look at the release notes of eml-codec 0.3.1 where the bulk of the work is done, building on eml-codec 0.2 for the initial setup of parsing recovery. Both shipped with Aerogramme 0.4.

IMAP's search and retrieval features are essential because they allow clients to have a snappy UX while handling mailboxes with thousands of emails. This post focused on getting those basic features right. But, more broadly, we think that the "mailbox as database" perspective is useful because it raises the question: which end-user workflows can we enable and support? Which features should we prioritize or optimize to best support the workflows of day-to-day email users?

Stay tuned for the next blogpost in the series where we discuss the other significant challenge for an IMAP server: mailbox concurrency!

Following the database analogy, the logical next step could be to optimize this by first "pre-compiling" queries before running them on emails. Right now we don't know if this optimization would actually matter in practice...

This links to IMAP4rev1 but the more recent IMAP4rev2 isn't more specific on this subject.

Latest Update: US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Commerce dept runing criminal investigation into Nvidia-linked Megaspeed.
  • The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has decided to ban remote access to certain GPUs and servers running in datacenters located in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
  • The agency has also introduced a requirement to secure a license before selling what it describes as “advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers” that are sufficiently powerful to “be used for training or running of advanced SI models” into the five nations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Commerce dept runing criminal investigation into Nvidia-linked Megaspeed.

The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has decided to ban remote access to certain GPUs and servers running in datacenters located in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

The agency has also introduced a requirement to secure a license before selling what it describes as “advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers” that are sufficiently powerful to “be used for training or running of advanced SI models” into the five nations.

The interim final rule [PDF] containing the new regulations says they’re needed “to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”.

Similar language can be found in previous US bans on sales of GPUs and other advanced tech to China, which Washington fears will use advanced tech to improve its military capabilities.

Sources indicate that US authorities understood that export bans wouldn’t prevent Chinese entities from renting GPUs housed elsewhere. So from 2021 to 2024, Washington introduced a series of regulations that required US-based clouds to make sure they didn’t serve Chinese customers.

In a recent development, no such obligation existed for cloud operators elsewhere, which created a market for resources that Chinese customers could access from afar. It is widely felt that datacenter building booms in Malaysia and Thailand, both of which are generally on good terms with China, aimed to cater to Middle Kingdom customers who wanted to rent GPUs they could not import.

Megapseed – whose former employee Alice Huang had an intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and may have been a Chinese intelligence asset – built datacenters in Malaysia and was suspected of catering largely to offshore customers.

Neil Shah, vice president of research at analyst firm Counterpoint, mentioned the upcoming rules shift the regulatory burden of complying with export controls from hardware manufacturers to cloud operators.

“Data center operators in hubs such as Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia will now face massive ‘Know Your Customer's Workload’ requirements,” he told The Register by email, likening it to the KYC restrictions imposed on financial services firms. “They must prove to US regulators that their compute is not being funneled back to embargoed nations, or risk losing their own access to US silicon.”.

He feels the fresh rules represent “a severe short-term compute bottleneck for Chinese tech giants” and “a massive long-term catalyst for decoupling.”.

“Washington is forcing domestic capital and engineering talent to double down on full-stack sovereign alternatives, accelerating ecosystems like Huawei's Ascend.”.

Shah’s observation came days after Alibaba decided to spin out its T-Head chip design unit, which it described as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China.” That description suggests Alibaba doesn’t think T-Head has strong prospects of selling its wares outside China.

In a recent development, it remains to be seen if the new BIS rules will slow datacenter development across Asia and Brazil. All five nations the US has regulated are all enjoying the economic impact of the AI boom. They’re also trying to manage its impact. Singapore limits datacenter construction, as befits a tiny and resource-constrained island nation. Malaysia is very much open for business but has introduced increasingly strict building codes and requirements to minimize energy and water consumption. Thailand recently introduced new regulations that new builds of large datacenters must take place in designated industrial zones. Indonesia also has strong regulations but is not currently a major datacenter hub.

Brazil requires datacenter operators to reserve at least 10 percent of capacity for local users, suggesting some operators are more interested in offshore customers.

Interestingly, the upcoming BIS rules don’t impact infrastructure used for “commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat.”.

It has been revealed that chinese e-tailers operate at vast scale and have already attracted regulatory attention in Europe and the USA. Asian and Brazilian datacenter operators therefore probably do not see the likes of Temu and Alibaba as a lifeline, but might see a role as regional hosts for outfits like Amazon or Meta. ®.

UDPATED AT 05:45 UTC, November 17 to add news that late on Monday the US Departments of Commerce and Justice confirmed an ongoing criminal investigation into Megaspeed.

In the announcement, the two departments detail investigative activities they conducted across 2024 and 2025, including a June meeting with Alice Huang in Singapore, and state those details "address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting.".

Singaporean authorities have also mentioned that meeting took place, but say they asked asked US counterparts for help with their own investigations and received frustratingly little support.

Singapore also investigated Supermicro's possible role at Megapseed, and complained that the server-maker didn't co-operate either.

Supermicro today told The Register it "does not conduct business with these entities" and operates a "robust compliance program.".

Industry observers note that "We are committed to complying with all applicable U.S. export and re-export control laws and regulations, and we require our distributors and resellers to do the same," according to a Supermicro statement sent to The Register.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet).
  • Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.
  • In a recent development, it's crucial to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

In a recent development, it's crucial to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

In a recent development, for Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:.

According to recent reports, today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:.

Recent findings suggest that the expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:.

For each vector generation, we record:.

Industry observers note that our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 newly introduced features:.

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Recent findings suggest that full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Sources indicate that we sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:.

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In a recent development, in our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

In a recent development, storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

It has been revealed that for us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:.

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:.

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

This gives us several useful properties:.

In a recent development, only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the upcoming generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:.

Recent findings suggest that the HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

According to recent reports, the Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:.

According to recent reports, if the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can rapidly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):.

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​.

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:.

Sources indicate that note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:.

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Industry observers note that because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Recent findings suggest that corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

According to recent reports, the revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

According to recent reports, scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

Sources indicate that new generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

The lexical fallback for scale-to-zero and the separate index activation boundary are useful production details. One question for the hybrid setup: do you measure relevance and latency separately when dense search is cold versus warm, so fallback quality is visible rather than hidden in an overall average? We examined lexical-first retrieval and semantic reranking on a smaller workload here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That benchmark doesn't establish behavior on a paper-scale corpus.

AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field.
  • Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.
  • AWS has debuted Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task, or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight virtual machine with a separate guest kernel, carved out of a running EC2 instance by the Nitro hypervisor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field.

Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.

AWS has debuted Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task, or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight virtual machine with a separate guest kernel, carved out of a running EC2 instance by the Nitro hypervisor. On Amazon EKS, the whole change is one pod field: runtimeClassName: isolated-sandbox or confidential-sandbox.

Recent findings suggest that the feature is available in all commercial regions at no additional charge, and AWS positions it for workloads where the tenant or the code cannot be trusted, with coding agents named first. In an AWS blog post, Carlos Santana and Trishi Mehta write:.

Each pod gets its own operating system, completely separate from the host and from every neighbor.

According to the EKS documentation, a containerd-shim-nitro-sandbox-v2 process on the parent instance debuts a Firecracker microVM as a first-level guest with hardware-assisted virtualization, after which an agent inside the VM runs the pod’s containers through its own containerd and the two sides communicate over virtio and vsock. The result is a sandbox that shares neither kernel nor memory mappings with the parent instance or any other sandbox, while the containers themselves start unchanged. How the nodes get there depends on the cluster type: on EKS Auto Mode the two RuntimeClasses ship with every cluster and sandbox-capable nodes are provisioned on demand, whereas on standard EKS a team builds a sandbox-enabled AMI for its node groups or Karpenter.

(Source: Amazon EKS User Guide).

What separates the two modes is which side of the boundary is trusted. Isolated mode trusts the parent instance and not the guest, which is why kubectl exec, logs, and process listing keep working, whereas confidential mode treats the parent as untrusted and moves enforcement inside the VM: a Cedar policy generated from the pod spec pins image digests, arguments, environment, mounts and capabilities, exec and stdin are denied, the Nitro Secure Module measures the image and policy into PCRs, and a KMS key policy can release secrets only to a sandbox whose measurements match. Image layers can be encrypted as well, so the parent moves ciphertext it never reads.

That chain only holds if something checks the measurements, and the documentation says so: without a KMS policy or external verifier checking the PCR values, "the attestation measurement is recorded but never verified, and the confidentiality guarantees of confidential mode are incomplete." Separately from either mode, a network-isolated annotation boots the sandbox with no network device at all, which also removes DNS, NTP, IMDS and Pod Identity and breaks HTTP and TCP probes.

Sandip Das, an AWS Container Hero, read the documentation the same way and drew out what isolated mode leaves to the operator: the protection "only runs in one direction," so a compromised parent can still observe or tamper with unencrypted traffic and DNS, writes the pod's /etc/hosts, and can mint Pod Identity credentials for any pod on the node. He also lists prerequisites the blog post does not, among them Kubernetes 1.36 or later, a launch template with Nitro Enclaves enabled on managed node groups, without which "sandboxed pods sit in Pending," and Pod Identity rather than IRSA for credentials. On AWS's description of performance as near-native, he advises treating it "as a vendor claim" and benchmarking startup latency, I/O throughput and tail latency.

Beyond agents, AWS lists multi-tenant SaaS, regulated workloads, CI builds and remote IDEs, and points to the open-source agent-sandbox project for warm pools that hand out a pre-booted VM in about two seconds.

The constraints are on the considerations page, and the largest is GPU and device passthrough, which is not supported at launch because Firecracker cannot pass host devices into a guest, so GPU pods run without the sandbox class. Density is capped twice over: total sandbox vCPUs may not exceed five times the node's vCPU count, and neither may the number of sandboxes, halved on CPU-overcommit types, which gives a 4-vCPU node room for twenty 1-vCPU sandboxes or five 4-vCPU ones. Simultaneous multithreading costs more than the arithmetic suggests, because core scheduling stops two sandboxes sharing the sibling threads of one core and leaves roughly half the advertised vCPUs usable; Graviton, with one thread per core, is unaffected.

According to recent reports, the nearest comparison is GKE Sandbox, which has offered a gvisor RuntimeClass since 2019 and more recently a microvm class built on Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor. gVisor intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel, starts in under 200 milliseconds and supports CUDA on a subset of GPUs; Google's microVM option carries a fixed 250 mCPU and 130 MiB per pod, starts in one to two seconds and does not support GPUs. AWS has taken the VM side of that split and expressed its overhead as density and threads rather than per-pod resources.

On EC2, Amazon Linux and Firecracker are supported natively and patches are available for other virtual machine monitors. The EC2 User Guide carries the supported instance list and notes that snapshot, restore and live migration are not available.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that most interesting AI apps are pipelines.
  • gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface.
  • The best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something new. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

The best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

👉 Try the Image Editor Pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that one graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Sources indicate that since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

Recent findings suggest that each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

According to recent reports, you get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

It has been revealed that every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

Decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

Check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

Sources indicate that every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:.

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:.

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:.

In a recent development, the fastest way in is to open any demo above, click Duplicate, and start rewiring. From Python, it is as short as:.

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

Sources indicate that you can even build something as involved as AUTOMATIC1111 with gr.Workflow. Keep an eye out for our next post, where we walk through building it step by step. Here is a sneak peek 😉👇.
