  • 9 Cybersecurity Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Practical guidance on safer search, stronger login security, better executive protection, and other habits can reduce enterprise risk.

9 Cybersecurity Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Threats.

According to recent reports, cybersecurity Awareness Month tends to bring no shortage of advice, but the most useful guidance for business readers is the kind that maps to the way attacks actually happen now: through everyday habits, trusted workflows, and small moments of inattention. Risks show up when employees trust a search result, follow a fake CAPTCHA prompt, scan a login QR code, click a social ad, reuse a weak recovery method, or assume that an artificial intelligence (AI) model, executive device, or home network is secure by default. This article, compiled by the Dark Reading staff, and the accompanying videos bring those risks together in one place and focus on the practical behaviors and controls that can reduce them.

Industry observers note that in October, a Dark Reading poll asked site visitors, "What's your biggest Cybersecurity Awareness Month challenge?" Readers identified phishing and social engineering as the top risk (39.1% of respondents), but that was neck-and-neck with shadow AI and risky data sharing (38.2%). A distant third was training fatigue and weak follow-through, identified as the top problem by 13.5% of respondents, and third-party and contractor access, with 9.2% of the vote.

Reader responses when asked, "What's your biggest Cybersecurity Awareness Month challenge?" Source: Dark Reading.

The following nine tips can move the dial on that enterprise risk in very real ways. A common thread for all of these is the fact that attackers win by abusing convenience, familiarity, and human trust, whether the matter is SEO poisoning, ClickFix, session hijacking, dark patterns, or dodgy ads on Facebook. That's why awareness training still matters. It shouldn't be a once-a-year affair either, but rather an everyday focus on a set of specific, repeatable habits backed by stronger enterprise safeguards.

For security leaders, Cybersecurity Awareness Month gives them the chance to do more than remind customers to "be careful." It is an opportunity to push for better defaults: phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA), tighter privilege controls, better reporting paths, safer browsing habits, stronger executive protection, and more realistic guidance for work that happens outside the office. The goal is to make the safe action the default action and to help employees recognize the red flags before a routine click becomes a business problem.

Embrace cybersecurity awareness in October and beyond with Dark Reading's curated hub for security leaders — featuring expert news, analysis, and insights for hardening enterprise defenses in areas like identity security, AI risk, social engineering, supply chain, and more.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Becky Bracken, Media & Projects Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

As enterprises look to embrace agentic AI, they're sorting through frontier models, open-weight alternatives, and overseas offerings. Much of the focus is on evaluating the safeguards that, say, Claude might have vs. an open-weight alternative, like Meta's Llama series. But for business leaders, the key question is not which model is inherently safe; it's whether your organization has put adequate controls around it. That means treating AI just like any other high-impact enterprise system that can be misconfigured, manipulated, abused, or compromised.

Recent findings suggest that every model type comes with trade-offs. Frontier models may offer stronger vendor tooling, safety features, and governance support, but they can also introduce concentration and third-party risk. Open-weight models can give enterprises more transparency and control, but that control comes with more responsibility for hardening, patching, monitoring, and misuse prevention. Either way, the burden is on the enterprise.

It has been revealed that for Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the practical takeaway is to assume compromise and build from there. Security teams should treat model weights, code, training data, prompts, plug-ins, APIs, and downstream applications as one attack surface. Limit what models can access. Restrict permissions. Segment AI workloads from critical systems. Log activity aggressively. Test for prompt injection, data leakage, and identity abuse. And keep humans in the loop for consequential actions, especially when money, customer data, or operational decisions are involved.

Industry observers note that this is a golden opportunity for cybersecurity teams to become business enablers in the best sense of the term. AI will move fast, vendors will keep promising better safeguards, and the market will keep generating noise. But the durable security advantage will come from steady internal discipline. AI models can help the business, but they cannot be trusted to protect the business.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Alex Culafi, Senior News Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Sources indicate that clickFix is a simple but effective attack because it exploits something security teams deal with every day: people trying to solve a problem quickly. The user lands on a compromised or malicious Web site, a phishing page, or a fake browser-based meeting screen and sees what looks like a normal verification or troubleshooting prompt.

But instead of asking them to check a box, the page tells them to open a system tool — often with Windows + R — and paste in a command that the site has already copied to their clipboard. Once they do, they can trigger the compromise themselves. Security researchers note that this technique has risen sharply and often relies on fake CAPTCHA or error messages that make the request seem routine.

No legitimate CAPTCHA, website, or meeting platform should ever ask a user to open Run, PowerShell, Terminal, or Command Prompt and paste in a script. A request like that should be treated as an immediate red flag. The attack works precisely because it looks like a harmless fix and can sidestep some browser-based protections by pushing the user to execute the command themselves.

Organizations should build this into awareness training now. Tell employees to stop immediately if a website asks them to copy and paste commands, press unusual key combinations, or "fix" an issue through a local system tool. Reinforce a simple rule: If a prompt moves from the browser into the operating system, assume it's suspicious until IT says otherwise. Also, make it easy to report these incidents fast because early notification can help security teams contain the damage and identify affected users quickly. Restricting access to system tools where appropriate can add another layer of defense.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Rob Wright, Senior News Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, here's a useful reminder for business leaders and employees alike: Treat social media ads as untrusted content. According to Gen Digital research, nearly one in three (31%) ads on Instagram and Facebook lead to scams, phishing pages, or malware.

And according to Reuters, Meta is charging higher premiums for advertisers that are considered risky. So not only have these platforms turned into a virtual minefield of scams, but Meta has a financial incentive to keep these ads online.

According to recent reports, that matters because malicious ads often don't look malicious. They may mimic legitimate brands, use convincing creative, and point to spoofed URLs that appear credible at first glance. Even security-aware users can get caught. The real danger is that these ads exploit trust, urgency, and familiarity — exactly the tactics that work on busy professionals who are clicking promptly on personal devices outside the protections of corporate security tools.

According to recent reports, caution remains the first line of defense. Encourage employees to use payment cards with fraud alerts, enable MFA on shopping and social accounts, and maintain healthy skepticism toward "limited-time" deals delivered through ad feeds.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Arielle Waldman, Features Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

According to recent reports, ransomware has moved beyond encrypting systems and stealing data. Increasingly, attackers are pressuring organizations by targeting the people around their leaders: spouses, children, relatives, and close friends.

It has been revealed that the "Semperis 2026 Ransomware Risk Report" found that 37% of attacks involved threats against employees' friends or family members. In other words, if attackers can't break your defenses fast enough, they may try to break your people instead. AI is accelerating this shift by making reconnaissance faster and cheaper, and threat actors can mine social media, public records, leaked data, and digital breadcrumbs to map relationships, impersonate trusted contacts, and build highly convincing social engineering campaigns.

According to recent reports, for Cybersecurity Awareness Month, organizations should expand executive protection beyond the corporate perimeter. Start with digital footprint reduction: Encourage executives and family members to limit public exposure, remove unnecessary personal details from social profiles, and use aliases or less identifiable display names where practical. Establish family verification procedures, including safe words or challenge-response phrases, but rotate them regularly because any phrase used in a compromised channel should be treated as burned.

Most importantly, extend basic cyber hygiene to the household. Require strong unique passwords, enforce MFA on personal and shared accounts, secure home networks and connected devices, and train family members to recognize urgency-based scams, impersonation attempts, and suspicious content. A child's gaming console, a spouse's reused password, or a relative's overshared profile can become the opening attackers need.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Fahmida Rashid, Editor-in-Chief at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Recent findings suggest that security awareness works better when it feels practical and relevant, not like a mandatory lecture. But one lesson is worth stating plainly: Some employees need more protection simply because they hold more power, more access, and more sensitive information. That starts with the C-suite, but it also applies to executive assistants, finance leaders, admins, and anyone else with privileged access.

A strong executive protection program should include:.

Phishing-resistant MFA, ideally hardware-based rather than SMS codes.

Just-in-time privileged access instead of standing elevated permissions.

Dedicated, locked-down devices for sensitive work.

Stronger email and DLP controls to catch unusual forwarding, sharing, or exfiltration patterns.

Focused coaching for executives and their inner circle, including assistants and chiefs of staff.

Guidance for family and home networks because executive risk doesn't stop at the office.

Sources indicate that organizations can focus on "white-glove" security, which means tighter controls, better support, and faster escalation when something looks off. If a control feels mildly annoying, that may be a sign it is doing its job.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Arielle Waldman, Features Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

These design tricks train people to click swiftly, surrender data reflexively, and ignore warning signs. Over time, that weakens judgment. Employees who get used to manipulative prompts may be less likely to notice when a request is truly malicious — whether that's a fake consent banner, a spoofed login page, a bogus app permission screen, or a prompt asking for sensitive information. Dark patterns blur the line between annoying and dangerous.

For organizations, the goal should be to treat dark-pattern awareness as part of security awareness. Start by reminding employees that convenience defaults are rarely the safest settings. Public profiles, broad calendar visibility, third-party integrations, and data-sharing permissions are often enabled by default. Employees should be encouraged to review privacy and sharing settings manually rather than assume the platform chose the secure option. It’s also worth checking authenticator app settings for too-broad sharing privileges.

In a recent development, finally, build a reporting culture around anything that feels off — surprise charges, mystery accounts, unusual permissions, or suspicious prompts. The more comfortable employees are raising small concerns, the easier it is to catch bigger complications before they spread.

Everyone knows password hygiene remains a challenge for most businesses, but risk in the login journey increasingly extends to the other seams around identity — the moments where people, devices, sessions, and recovery workflows intersect.

The threats include quishing, where a user scans a QR code from an email, Web page, or physical sign and lands on a convincing but malicious login screen. There's also push fatigue, where attackers bombard a user with approval requests until one gets accepted. And it includes session hijacking and token theft, where the attacker skips the password entirely and hops into an already authenticated session. Add SIM swapping to intercept SMS-based recovery, and the modern login chain starts to look brittle in several different places.

The long-term fix is to move toward phishing-resistant authentication, including FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, backed by enterprise controls that verify context, not just credentials. That requires checking device posture, monitoring session behavior, requiring managed devices for sensitive systems, and reauthenticating when risk changes. In short: Don't just trust the login — trust the device, the session, and the user behavior behind it.

However, if this kind of full passkey rollout is not on the docket yet, here are some practical steps organizations can take now to reduce login risk:.

Turn on number matching for push-based MFA.

Reduce or eliminate SMS-based authentication where possible.

Throttle repeated approval prompts.

Shorten session lifetimes for high-risk apps.

Require managed-device access for sensitive systems.

Trigger reauthentication when device posture changes.

Meanwhile, employee training should focus on a few clear habits: Don't scan login QR codes from unsolicited messages or unverified sources, for one, and never approve an unexpected SMS verification push.

It has been revealed that to prevent session hijacking, log out of accounts when you finish using them, rather than just closing the browser tab. And avoid public Wi-Fi when you're doing something sensitive.

Finally, on the SIM-swapping front, switch from SMS MFA to Authenticator Apps that can't be intercepted via a phone network. You can also request that account changes require physical ID in-store or multilayered, out-of-band authentication before processing SIM changes.

Account takeover attacks are a bugbear that is unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but increasing friction and cost for attackers throughout the login process can truly help and, hopefully at the very least, get you out of the low-hanging-fruit category.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Rob Wright, Senior News Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

It has been revealed that fall youth sports season means many parent-professionals are working from the sidelines — at soccer fields, hockey rinks, football stadiums, and school gyms — often on whatever free Wi-Fi happens to be available. That may not sound as risky as logging on at a major airport or hotel, but it still creates an opportunity for mistakes that attackers, pranksters, or opportunistic snoops can exploit.

Industry observers note that so, although sophisticated nation-state actors are probably not camping out at your local rink, there's still considerable risk if you connect to the wrong network. A hotspot with a name that closely resembles the venue's legitimate Wi-Fi can be enough to trick a busy parent checking email between periods or joining a meeting from the bleachers. Even a spoofed network set up as a joke can expose traffic, credentials, or session data if employees are careless.

Business readers that want to avoid their employer's penalty box should treat public connectivity anywhere as untrusted by default. Before joining a network, verify the exact Wi-Fi name with venue staff or posted signage. Disable auto-join so your device does not connect to similarly named networks without your knowledge. Use only approved secure remote access tools, keep endpoint protections enabled, and avoid handling sensitive work, such as admin access, financial approvals, or password resets, over public Wi-Fi unless it is absolutely necessary.

Recent findings suggest that if you need connectivity, a personal hotspot is often the safer option — but only if it is configured properly. Use a strong password, change the default network name if it reveals your identity, and make sure the hotspot is not left open to nearby devices.

The broader lesson for Cybersecurity Awareness Month: Low-profile locations can still produce real security failures. The setting may feel routine, but the network risk is not.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Alex Culafi, Senior News Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

SEO poisoning turns a routine Google search into an attack path. Threat actors either build lookalike websites or compromise legitimate ones, then manipulate content and code so those pages rank highly in search results. The idea is that a user searching for software, a login page, or a partner site might simply click the top result, which happens to be poisoned, and subsequently hand over credentials or download malware.

Guidance on spotting fake websites specifically warns that SEO poisoning can push malicious sites to the top of search results, and Trend Micro's 2026 research on more than 35,000 fake World Cup-related sites reveals how easily attackers can industrialize fake-site campaigns around high-interest topics.

Recent findings suggest that for business users, the safest habit is to stop trusting search rankings as a signal of legitimacy. Before clicking, inspect the URL for misspellings, extra words, odd country codes, or brand names that look slightly off. After clicking, be suspicious if the page immediately pushes a download, asks for credentials too early, triggers repeated redirects, throws pop-ups, or trips a browser warning. Those are strong signs that something is wrong.

Organizations should reinforce a few simple rules in awareness training:.

Use bookmarks or manually typed URLs for key business apps, vendors, and partner portals.

Verify domains before downloading software or entering credentials.

Treat urgent install prompts and so-called ClickFix instructions as red flags.

Report suspicious search results, spoofed pages, and accidental downloads to IT immediately.

Isolate the device and change credentials promptly if a user may have interacted with a fake site.

In a recent development, the practical message for Cybersecurity Awareness Month: Search is a convenience layer, not a trust layer. Employees don't need to become threat hunters, but they do need to slow down long enough to verify where a search result is actually taking them. That pause can prevent a compromise.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

According to recent reports, an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

Industry observers note that an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that demonstrates up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, customers of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a fresh paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

It has been revealed that the frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

According to recent reports, the RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Sources indicate that framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

It has been revealed that the viewer reveals the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

According to recent reports, here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

It has been revealed that A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

It has been revealed that neMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

It has been revealed that the best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

It has been revealed that that is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

Sources indicate that the first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

It has been revealed that the bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your consumers publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christoph Hellwig has revealed the initial public release of XRAID—declustered parity RAID that is integrated into XFS.

Recent findings suggest that the two primary aims of XRAID are to support parity RAID on zoned devices like SMR hard drives, and to provide a fast RAID implementation without inherent data integrity problems. XRAID, just like zoned XFS also works on conventional hard drives and SSDs. Optimizing for SSD performance has not been a focus, but even without that, writes are up to 20 times faster than mdraid. [...].

According to recent reports, work on XRAID has been ongoing for a year and a half, and while we aren't anywhere near ready for an upstream submission, we are interested in feedback and testing from a wider audience now. The current implementation supports zero to 2 parities. We did experiments with the SnapRAID parity library to support 3 and more parities, and while that is not included in the current version, support for more parities is planned and the code is prepared for it.

The xfsprogs branch includes mkfs support and a new "xraid" utility for managing devices and inspecting an XRAID file-systems. We have also extended Zonar (The zoned file-system visualisation tool) to show how each logical zone maps onto physical zones on devices.

Hellwig gave a presentation at FOSSY in August on this topic; video of the talk does not seem to be available yet, but his slides are available.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MountAIn revealed €7.3 million in seed financing on November 17, 2026, to commercialize MountainCore, its platform for running complete computer-vision applications on microcontrollers costing less than $10.

The financing came from 360 Capital, Supernova Invest and Crédit Agricole Alpes Développement, with additional support from Bpifrance. MountAIn plans to expand its engineering team in Grenoble, strengthen its presence in Europe and Silicon Valley, and target semiconductor, smart-camera and industrial-equipment manufacturers.

In a recent development, mountAIn is addressing the gap between a trained model and the limited processors inside cameras, industrial equipment and other connected devices. Memory and power are constrained, connectivity can be unreliable, and hardware-specific integration can turn deployment into a lengthy engineering program. Buying powerful, energy-hungry hardware increases costs, while sending data to the cloud adds expense, latency, connectivity requirements and privacy concerns.

MountainCore adapts the model and its supporting software together and supports multiple ARM-based microcontroller families. The organization’s product site describes the underlying MountAIn Core as a developer workflow, compiler and middleware layer that optimizes the full application path for its target environment. Its Onboard route is intended to bring a model into an existing board, camera, sensor or device stack without rebuilding the product around a upcoming AI platform.

MountAIn says the platform can reduce deployment engineering from months to hours, cut model memory requirements by up to threefold, make better use of on-chip AI accelerators and preserve accuracy without retraining. Applications then run on the device, reducing cloud costs and keeping sensitive data local.

Recent findings suggest that “AI models are designed for GPUs and data centers, yet most equipment in the real world could run on microcontrollers consuming just milliwatts of power,” remarked Vincent Huard, MountAIn’s CEO and co-founder. He said the financing is intended to turn early industrial use into large-scale commercial deployment.

Teledyne e2v demonstrated MountainCore at VISION Stuttgart in 2026, using it in an edge-AI system that combined 2D and 3D vision from its Perciva 5D camera. Roboflow, whose platform MountAIn notes is used by more than two million developers and 80,000 companies, now offers direct model export to IBEX. Alif Semiconductor has also partnered with MountAIn on computer-vision applications for its energy-efficient Ensemble and Balletto processor families.

Recent findings suggest that IBEX demonstrates how the technology can operate in remote, off-grid locations. MountAIn says the autonomous vision sensor consumes less than 100 milliwatts and was named a CES 2026 Innovation Awards Honoree. Solar-powered and satellite-connected, IBEX analyzes images locally for applications such as early wildfire detection and infrastructure monitoring.

MountAIn plans to return to CES in Las Vegas in January 2027 to demonstrate MountainCore’s industrial capabilities and show IBEX applications designed for remote locations.

For MountAIn, the central commercial question is whether those partner integrations and demonstrations can become large-scale deployments while preserving model accuracy and delivering the engineering-time savings the tech giant reports on constrained hardware.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holo4 is our fresh series of agentic models.
  • In a recent development, holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • It has been revealed that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holo4 is our fresh series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

In a recent development, holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

It has been revealed that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Sources indicate that holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

It has been revealed that no one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Sources indicate that our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Recent findings suggest that alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

Industry observers note that these gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

Breaking: Github Redesign (2019)

📅 28 Feb 2019 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tonsky

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Github design is pretty good: it gets the job done, it’s clean, has consistent visual language, its design is calm and suitable for everyday use.
  • Given all that, there are still many areas that could be improved.
  • Industry observers note that let’s start with the biggest problem right away: information architecture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Github design is pretty good: it gets the job done, it’s clean, has consistent visual language, its design is calm and suitable for everyday use.

Given all that, there are still many areas that could be improved. Today we’ll take one interface—repository page—and look what UI problems it has and if we can fix them.

Industry observers note that let’s start with the biggest problem right away: information architecture. Take tabs. Currently there’re two levels of tabs, one nested under the other:.

It has been revealed that if you are a programmer, you might be surprised but other people normally don’t like hierarchies. Nested structures are hard to grasp, remember, navigate, and grouping is very often non-intuitive. Nested tabs are one of the worst UI patterns out there.

According to recent reports, then there’s a plain usability matter: let’s say I’m in Wiki and need to see Releases. What should I do? There’s no Releases tab visible, so I must figure out somehow that Releases are part of the Code (?). That makes almost no sense. Releases are as much part of the Code as Challenges or Wiki are.

Solution here is to flatten all tabs into a single navigational control:.

In a recent development, organized that way, tabs are immediately accessible from anywhere in the repo. This is a massive deal.

As a bonus, we also won quite a bit of vertical space without sacrificing anything! Vertical space is very important, it lets you see more content and get to it faster—all good things.

Sources indicate that we still have one problem though: tabs don’t fit. We’re going to solve it by removing icons, but let me build up a case for that first.

Icons are visual cues that help you scan the UI promptly. “Quickly” here means faster than reading text labels. If for some reason reading labels is still faster then icons aren’t working.

One example of icons misuse: if you put too many icons in a row and they are all different, they won’t work.

In a recent development, prioritizing, or highlighting, something means deprioritizing everything else. You can’t highlight everything.

Another way to fail at icons: if you use obscure graphics, people will have to read labels anyways, so, again, not working.

Now let’s be honest: the domain of repository and project management is pretty abstract. No matter how good you are at design and how hard you try, you won’t come up with a great icon for a commit. Or a release. Or an matter. Or a license. A great icon is something other people know and understand. And for repositories, there’s simply none. I mean,.

So Github tab icons are purely decorative. If you don’t believe me, look at what Github itself is doing. They dim icons:.

That’s a sure sign that they, too, think it’s near impossible to figure out why backward clock means “Commit”. Github knows people will be looking at the labels anyways.

Recent findings suggest that but even being decorative, they’re bad at it. I mean, Icon + Label + Counter make for a symmetric and weak composition:.

It has been revealed that win-win-win! Here’s the result, tabs without icons:.

Test yourself, see if you can find Releases tab without an icon and if it was harder than before? It wasn’t, was it?

Recent findings suggest that A note on this design: I am using the same limitations Github already uses: English language only, locked page width of 1020px. For different conditions, say, for the adaptive design we might want a different solution.

Another note: I had to remove Contributors tab (which was actually not a tab, but a sub-tab from Insights that was duplicated in Code for some reason) to accommodate for Settings tab. Don’t worry, we’ll get Contributors back later.

It has been revealed that the thing with vanity metrics is that there should be just one. One metrics is simple to understand and focus. Two or three split attention, making everything weaker.

According to recent reports, luckily for us, both watchers and forks perform poorly as metrics anyways. For watches, people tend not to watch too much. For forks, people tend to fork for no reason.

But stars work. They work because they have no other function but to represent vanity. So let’s keep stars and move them to the left to get more attention:.

In a recent development, in the watch button we have a classic “button or status” UX dilemma. Buttons tell us what can be done but don’t say what the current status is. Status tells current state but it’s not clear what it would change to.

Sources indicate that in Github case “Watch” has a button label but it doesn’t act as a button: clicking on it won’t make you watch the repo. It’s not a status either: if you see “Watch” it means you are not watching. Same for the other two states: they are neither buttons nor states.

It has been revealed that the problem here is that a single button can’t be used to switch between three states. But dropdown can! Dropdowns are a well-established UI component that shows status and can be used to change it at the same time.

In a recent development, funny, but Github is already using a dropdown! We just need to fix it to work as any other dropdown on Earth works: to show current status. Trivial fix, really:.

Minor, but annoying: that checkmark is really hard to spot. Let’s highlight the whole row:.

According to recent reports, uff, we’ve done a lot! If you need a little break, now would be a perfect time for it. Don’t worry, I’ll wait.

This is the repository description:.

The problem with it is: why is it located under the Code tab? It’s a description of the whole repository, not just its code, right?

To fix this let’s move it above the tabs, to the area that belongs to the whole repository:.

It still needs a couple of touches.

Sources indicate that first, font is neither big nor small (it’s 16px, standing between 18px repository name and 14px tabs). Let’s make it 14px so that there’re only two distinct font sizes. Also I’m sure there’s no need to render “https://” in the URL:.

In a recent development, the second change is to move topics right next to the repository name. There’re usually just a few of those, so it seems wasteful to dedicate a whole line to them:.

Look at us, winning more vertical space again!

Industry observers note that blue topics on blue background became harder to read. This is because they used to be on #FFF and now they’re on Github’s #FAFBFC “very light dirty blue”.

Let’s change tab’s background to #FFF too:.

But why was that background there in the first place? What did it do?

My guess is Github had to add it because the structure of their menu layers was becoming too complex and they needed visual cues to help you “split” it in order to understand. The black top bar serves the same purpose: to separate. I mean, they were literally spending a good half of 768px screen at navigation alone.

When split into layers, at least you are not immediately scared by it. Without a background, it would be a mess.

But because we simplified the whole header so much and removed one intermediate layer, we don’t need that color coding anymore. Instead, we can enjoy fresh crisp white:.

And look at all that free space! Finally, we can see some content in the top half of the screen too.

Recent findings suggest that A small touch. If you own the repository, you get to edit both its description and its topics:.

First, the “Edit” button is badly misplaced — too far, easy to miss.

Second, separate edit button for topics is an artifact of topics system being developed at a different time, maybe by a different team. There’s really no need to have two separate buttons.

According to recent reports, the solution? How many edit buttons do we need? I say none.

“But... Where did edit buttons go?” You might ask.

You see, the nature of description and topics is that it’s important to get people to fill them when they first create their repo. After that, people rarely change them at all.

When there is no description or no topics, we will show a button to add one:.

According to recent reports, and if description/topics are already filled, go to Settings to change them. Problem solved!

The traditional Windows File Explorer, together with macOS Finder, have established a simple pattern for file browsing: files on the left, details on the right.

Github decided to copy that pattern, but they put a very unexpected thing as details: a message from the last commit when that particular file was changed.

Sources indicate that why? I don’t know. Commits often touch files for completely arbitrary reasons, so the last commit tells you almost nothing. I can’t think of any case when somebody would need that particular information.

It has been revealed that maybe they wanted Github to be “about git” more than about traditional file browsing, and this was the only thing they could think of? That’s my speculation, anyway.

The problem with those details is not that such a huge area is filled with something so rarely useful. The problem is that it looks so much like file description it confuses me every time. “Tweak layout” is not a description of the “Docs” folder. “Need these debug tools too” for “Tools”—why should I care?

That means we can get rid of the descriptions without really losing anything:.

Industry observers note that when you get to the repository, the first page you see should not necessarily be Code. We better call it Overview—something to get a quick idea of what’s going on.

According to recent reports, now, the Github repository is more than just a list of files. It’s also about how those files change over time. What latest features were added? Which bugs were fixed? Were there any new releases recently? All those are as crucial as the files themselves.

That’s why I suggest we add a list of recent commits to the Overview page next to files.

You can now see if a project is actively developed, maintained or abandoned, if an matter you care about was recently fixed, if a upcoming version was recently published etc (notice tags and branches pills in commit list—I miss this feature on Commits tab SO MUCH).

Industry observers note that what about that free space on the right? We can put useful stats there:.

First, I added contributors. Github is all about people and collaboration, that’s why they put so much emphasis on Fork and PR buttons. Well, people are the face of that collaboration. They put their free time and energy to make that code happen. It’s only fair to see some of their faces.

Activity is a relatively latest feature that hasn’t found its place on repository page yet—until now. Helps you see how much momentum the project has.

It has been revealed that language statistics was unfairly hidden away, now it’s front and foremost. I also added code size in lines of code — an obvious addition that Github still doesn’t have for some reason.

Altogether, in my opinion, the new Overview tab is more helpful in everyday use.

Both “Create fresh file”, “Upload files” and “Find files” all relate to files, so it will be reasonable to move them right next to the thing they operate on: Files.

Github always used to have clone URL directly on a page. That was pretty useful—when you needed to grab the code, no additional clicks were required.

Unfortunately, during one of the redesigns Github hid the clone URL behind a button. My guess is they did it because there was simply not enough space. But people kept looking for it so they had to paint the button green.

Well, after moving file buttons we have enough space to restore full-length Clone link:.

I also unified all four ways to get the repo into a single control, because semantically they are pretty much the same: a way to get the code on your machine.

This is how Github used to look back in 2013:.

And this is a screenshot from 2015:.

Finally, this is how it looks today:.

It has been revealed that as you can see, the color scheme and main UI elements haven’t changed much since at least 2013. It’s not necessarily bad and mostly proves that the original design was good enough to stand the test of time.

According to recent reports, but maybe it’s time to fresh it up a little? Get rid of gradients, dirty washed-out colors, unnecessary separators, add a little more air. Something like this:.

In a recent development, if you feel disoriented, give it a minute. Once you are used to it, you might notice it’s actually easier on the eyes and a bit lighter.

Current Github design next to my proposal:.

We’ve added ~4 more files to the screen of the same vertical size, 6 last commits, 3 branches, 10 contributors’ faces, project activity AND expanded language stats WITHOUT losing any information.

If you know someone at Github, send them a link to this article. Maybe someone there will like my ideas and eventually get to implement them—who knows?

Ten Years On, Google Updates the SRE Book for the AI Era

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Ten Years On, Google Updates the SRE Book for the AI Era.
  • Nov 17, 2026 5 min read.
  • Google has announced a completely rewritten second edition of their seminal book Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems, ten years after the original book was first published.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Ten Years On, Google Updates the SRE Book for the AI Era.

Nov 17, 2026 5 min read.

Google has announced a completely rewritten second edition of their seminal book Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems, ten years after the original book was first published. The book updates thinking on site reliability engineering (SRE) to encompass modern cloud architectures, platform engineering and AI workloads, whilst keeping the original emphasis on applying good software engineering techniques to operations work.

In a recent development, revealed by Google's SRE programme manager Betsy Beyer and software engineer David Huska, the upcoming edition is positioned as a response to a production environment that has changed substantially since 2016, when the first edition appeared. The authors argue that the central problem is no longer adopting cloud infrastructure, but maintaining reliability as systems become more distributed, interdependent and continuously changing.

It has been revealed that the original SRE book became influential because it gave a public account of how Google operated large-scale services. It described practices such as service level objectives (SLOs), error budgets, toil reduction, incident management and postmortems. InfoQ's 2016 review noted that the book presented SRE as the application of software engineering to an operations function, with engineers expected to automate repetitive operational work rather than simply respond to it.

The second edition does not present SRE as a fixed set of practices. Instead, it describes how those practices have changed as organisations have moved from early cloud migration and monolithic applications towards microservices, multi-cloud deployments, serverless systems and internal developer platforms.

One of the clearest changes over the years concerns SLOs and error budgets. Google notes that teams once relied on basic availability metrics and manually applied error-budget policies. The revised guidance describes user-centred, multi-tiered SLOs, dynamic burn-rate alerting and automated policy enforcement. Reliability practice itself has evolved away from infrastructure uptime alone and towards measures that describe the effect of failures on users.

Sources indicate that observability has also evolved, and the book's new edition talks this through. The first edition's world of static dashboards, basic logs and manual alert triage has given way, in Google's account, to OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing and automated anomaly correlation. The aim is not merely to collect more telemetry, but to reduce the time between an alert and a credible explanation of what has failed.

Automation is the third major area of revision. Google describes a movement from custom scripts addressing isolated tasks towards declarative infrastructure as code, internal developer platforms and self-healing systems. This aligns with the platform-engineering model now common in larger organisations: reliability capabilities are built once into a platform and consumed by product teams, rather than being reimplemented by every team.

Sources indicate that reliability testing has also changed. Google contrasts scheduled game days and synthetic load tests with continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing and live production canary verification. The practical implication is that resilience becomes part of the delivery pipeline rather than an occasional exercise performed before a major release.

Industry observers note that capacity management is another area where the book has been updated. Google states that manual provisioning and static forecasting have been replaced by dynamic auto-scaling, cloud FinOps alignment and optimisation for GPU and TPU clusters. This matters because AI training and inference workloads can concentrate demand on scarce accelerated computing resources, making capacity planning, networking and cost control more operationally significant.

Generative AI inevitably appears in the second edition, in two facets. First, SRE is presented as a discipline needed to operate AI infrastructure. The book covers the reliability of large GPU and TPU clusters, network topologies, non-deterministic model outputs, latency behaviour and the pipelines used for training, fine-tuning and data processing. These are different operational problems from those posed by a conventional stateless web service.

Second, AI is presented as a tool for reliability engineers. The post welcomes generative AI support for incident triage and postmortem writing, natural-language queries over telemetry, and predictive models that identify resource bottlenecks before they cause an outage. The examples in the announcement mostly place AI in a supporting role, gathering and organising evidence for engineers, rather than claiming that AI can replace operational judgement. Recent industry activity appears to support this, with InfoQ reporting in October 2026 that Datadog had released Scout, a specialist model intended to investigate production problems inside its Bits AI SRE product. Other vendors are exploring similar territory, including Honeycomb's Canvas Agent, Splunk AI SRE and New Relic's SRE Agent. InfoQ also reported in February 2026 on Google Cloud SREs using the Gemini CLI during real outages; using AI to help engineers work through incidents, rather than as an autonomous replacement for on-call staff.

The announcement also revises the organisational side of SRE. Google describes a move beyond dedicated SRE teams attached to particular applications, towards hybrid models, platform-engineering integration and reliability champions embedded in product teams. This has come about because many organisations cannot staff a central SRE team for every service, so reliability expertise has to be distributed more widely.

According to recent reports, despite the technological updates, Google argues that the underlying culture has not changed. The authors restate the importance of reliability-focused culture and expand the book's coverage of the human aspects of systems engineering. David Blank-Edelman made a related point in a presentation, You Are Asking the Wrong Questions (about Reliability and SRE), delivered at InfoQ Dev Summit Boston in 2025. He argued that reliability work should start from the customer's perspective rather than the component's perspective, and described SRE as fundamentally collaborative. He also challenged the conventional focus on a single root cause, favouring an examination of the contributing factors behind a failure.

The second edition is available in physical format through Google Books and in digital format from O'Reilly. For teams already practising SRE, its value is likely to lie less in introducing familiar concepts than in showing how those concepts have been adapted for platforms, distributed systems and AI-heavy infrastructure. For organisations earlier in their reliability journey, it remains a substantial reference on how to make operations a software-engineering problem rather than a collection of manual tasks.

Tech Report: Sadeepa Wijesekara, Vice President of Private Cloud AI at HPE – Interview Series

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sadeepa Wijesekara is Vice President of Private Cloud AI at Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), where he leads work on enterprise AI software and platforms for private cloud environments.
  • Industry observers note that hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) provides enterprise technology spanning AI, cloud, networking, compute, and storage.
  • HPE has scaled AI adoption across more than 70,000 employees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sadeepa Wijesekara is Vice President of Private Cloud AI at Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), where he leads work on enterprise AI software and platforms for private cloud environments. His focus includes helping organizations deploy AI securely and at scale while connecting infrastructure decisions with the needs of the business. He brings an engineering perspective to the economics of production AI, including workload management, model selection, and the costs of keeping increasingly autonomous systems reliable.

Industry observers note that hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) provides enterprise technology spanning AI, cloud, networking, compute, and storage. Its Private Cloud AI portfolio supports organizations deploying AI workloads on infrastructure they control, alongside hybrid cloud and external services. In this interview, Wijesekara discusses why AI spending should be measured against business outcomes, how agentic workflows change consumption, and the financial and operational factors that shape decisions about models, orchestration, and infrastructure.

HPE has scaled AI adoption across more than 70,000 employees. What has that experience taught you about when AI economics stops being an IT concern and becomes a broader business discipline?

AI economics becomes a broader business discipline when companies move from pilots into production. A pilot can show whether AI can perform a task, but it can hide inefficiencies because the number of users is small. Once you move from 10 users to 10,000, you have to think about cost, latency and reliability while also understanding the value the AI is creating. At that point, the conversation needs to include finance and the leaders responsible for the business processes AI supports. IT can measure the resources an application consumes, but business leaders need to determine whether the results justify that investment.

It has been revealed that many organizations still focus heavily on metrics such as cost per token when evaluating generative AI. Why do you believe cost per business outcome is a more meaningful measure, and how should enterprises calculate it in practice?

Cost per token tells you how much AI you consumed, but it does not tell you whether that consumption produced a useful result. Companies should define the business outcome first and then calculate the total cost required to produce it. The model is one part of that cost, alongside software, storage, data movement, governance and people. Comparing those costs with the value created within a specific business process gives companies a better picture of whether the investment makes economic sense.

As AI moves from individual copilots toward agentic and multi-agent systems that can perform lengthy sequences of tasks, how dramatically could consumption increase even if the underlying cost of inference continues to decline?

According to recent reports, consumption can rise very rapidly because one user request may trigger much more work behind the scenes. An agent can retrieve information and call tools while working through several steps before producing a result. In one representative HPE comparison, a basic chatbot exchange used about 400 tokens while an agentic RAG request used about 21,500. Even if token prices decline, total consumption can still increase sharply as AI takes on more complex work.

How should companies evaluate whether an AI use case is genuinely creating economic value rather than simply increasing productivity metrics or generating impressive demonstrations?

In a recent development, A use case should be tied to a business case with clear KPIs before it scales. Companies need to understand what the business process costs and how that changes when AI is introduced. They also need to distinguish between an improvement in an activity and an improvement in the business result. Time saved becomes more meaningful when it translates into resolving more customer concerns, reducing errors or completing work that previously went undone. The evaluation should account for the quality of the result and any additional review or rework required. A successful demonstration proves a capability; measurable improvements in the business process support the decision to expand it. In some cases, that analysis may show that AI is not the right answer.

Model routing and AI orchestration are increasingly being discussed as ways to control costs. How much value can enterprises unlock by dynamically choosing between smaller models, frontier models, specialized models, and traditional software depending on the task?

There is a lot of value in matching the model to the task. We have seen companies send very different workloads to the same expensive frontier model because their initial priority was getting AI up and running. That may be manageable with a small number of owners, but the cost grows promptly as adoption expands. A frontier model may make sense for complex reasoning, while a smaller model may be enough for a routine task. A specialized model may be better suited to a particular domain, and a predictable, rules-based task may be handled more efficiently by traditional software. Orchestration helps bring those choices together within a workflow, using a more capable model when the task requires it. As open-weight models become more capable, companies also have more opportunities to run certain workloads on their own infrastructure rather than paying for external models. At enterprise scale, those routing decisions can make a significant difference in cost while maintaining the quality the business requires.

According to recent reports, at what point does the economics of running AI workloads shift from renting compute through an API or public cloud toward owning or controlling more of the underlying infrastructure? What variables should enterprises consider when making that decision?

I think of it as renting versus buying. Renting can make sense while companies are experimenting or when demand varies significantly. As usage becomes larger and more predictable, owning or controlling more of the infrastructure can start to make economic sense. Owning infrastructure also creates opportunities to run additional AI experiments during periods of low usage, making better use of an investment already made. Companies need to consider the characteristics of the workload as well as the costs of power, management and keeping systems current. For many large enterprises, the right approach will likely include both private infrastructure and external services depending on the workload.

In a recent development, HPE has been expanding its private AI infrastructure as enterprises move more workloads into production. Where do you see private AI having the strongest economic advantage compared with consuming AI entirely through public cloud services?

According to recent reports, private AI can have a strong economic advantage for sustained workloads where companies can make effective use of the capacity they own. In one HPE analysis under specified workload assumptions, HPE Private Cloud AI was estimated at about $45 per node-hour compared with about $102 for an equivalent rented cloud configuration. Those results will vary by workload and should be recalculated for each environment. Private AI also gives companies another financial model, allowing infrastructure to become an asset that produces value for the organization.

In a recent development, AI agents introduce costs that extend beyond inference, including data retrieval, tool calls, monitoring, security, and governance. What costs are organizations most likely to underestimate when budgeting for agentic AI at scale?

Recent findings suggest that I think companies are likely to underestimate the work required to keep agents reliable, secure and useful over time. Beyond inference, there are costs associated with retrieving and preparing data, accessing external tools and moving information between systems. Repeated tool calls or failed attempts can add expense without producing a completed task. Companies also need to budget for evaluating results, monitoring agent behavior, managing access permissions and maintaining security and governance controls. Human oversight belongs in that calculation as well, including the time people spend reviewing exceptions or correcting errors. Understanding the cost of a successfully completed task requires visibility into that entire workflow.

It has been revealed that you’ve emphasized tracking AI consumption against individual business cases. What does an effective internal measurement framework look like, and how frequently should organizations reassess whether an AI application still justifies its ongoing compute and operating costs?

It has been revealed that the framework should connect usage directly to the business case. Companies need to know which application is consuming resources and what result it is expected to produce. At HPE, we track KPIs and underlying unit costs for each use case to measure whether it is delivering the expected results. I would also want to see that at the level of individual departments and business processes, so a CFO can understand what a process costs today compared with what it costs with AI. This should be an ongoing process because usage and the economics of an application can change over time. Companies should also reassess when a model, price or workflow changes materially, because those changes can affect both the cost and the value of an application.

Looking three to five years ahead, as AI becomes embedded across most business processes, how do you expect enterprise AI economics to evolve? Will managing AI consumption eventually resemble disciplines such as cloud FinOps, or will organizations need an entirely fresh operating model?

I think AI economics will build on FinOps disciplines such as cost visibility, allocation and accountability, while extending them to measure the quality and value of the work AI performs. As agents take on more steps within a business process, companies will need to understand the cost of completing that process successfully, including retries, human intervention and whether the result meets the required standard. I expect that to become a shared responsibility across IT, finance and business operations. We are still early in establishing consistent ways to make those comparisons across organizations and industries. Over time, I would like to see standard measures that allow companies to understand how efficiently they are operating with AI and reflect that in their P&L.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to learn more about private cloud AI, enterprise infrastructure, and scaling AI workloads should visit HPE.
