It doesn't necessarily mean that for your use case, it's going to work very well. That's how we approach the problem. We didn't treat inference as a solved problem. We started looking into what is different in our workload and what are all the optimization opportunities we can look out for. In the next few slides, I'm going to dive deeper into the inference side of things. The whole idea here is there are a lot of bottlenecks, not inference related, but system related, runtime related, maybe related to the engine you are serving, maybe related to the language you are serving, which I am going to call out.

According to recent reports, these might be hiding in your stack as well. The first bottleneck was on the CPU side. When you are serving production systems using LLMs, the first step is something called a tokenizer. In our code, what we had was we were taking the batch of items. Let's go back to the ranking workload. You have a request where you want to rank 50 items, let's say. You have like 50 prompts as a batch input to the LLM. In our code, what was happening was the tokenizer was happening sequentially on the CPU side. Basically, this was happening in the for loop one by one, it was stalling the GPU and the CPU was just sitting idle. In order to fix this, we replaced this with a batch tokenizer. What it means is Hugging Face APIs provide a fast tokenizer API, where you can send a batch of prompts and then it will parallelize the work across multiple codes.

Internally, it's implemented using REST, but for our use case, all this is available in open source. You just have to leverage these APIs. A natural extension of this was, can we do something on the server side so that we don't have to repeat this client-side batching for workloads where clients cannot naturally batch and send a batch request. We did have a lot of embedding generation workloads where either the client was not able to batch on the client side, or we had a shared model where we had multiple clients. If you want to do this batching on the client side, you have to repeat this logic across multiple clients. That's where we introduced something like server-side batching, which is going to batch across the request and then do one batch tokenization using the same fast tokenizer API, which I mentioned before. The important callout here is, if you are having any production systems, make sure you are doing batch tokenization. All these APIs are available out there in open source. Just make sure you are leveraging them.

In a recent development, the next bottleneck was even more subtle. When you are having an LLM based system, as I mentioned, you will have the tokenizer process, which is going to take the prompt and then figure out the token IDs. There will also be a scheduler process, some sort of scheduler, which is the one which is preparing the work and then dispatching the work to the GPU. Then we profiled the system and then figured out the root cause here to be the inter-process communication between these two processes. Essentially, from the tokenizer process to the scheduler process, we were sending the prompts one by one in a separate ZMQ message. In order to fix this, again, the fixes here are really simple.

Recent findings suggest that you just want to maintain the batch integrity throughout. You just send all of them in a single ZMQ message, so that the entire batch is passed on from the tokenizer to the scheduler in one shot. A key takeaway from this slide is, if you are having production systems based in Python, you are definitely leveraging multiprocessing for some reason. I'll discuss about why in the next few slides. Make sure when you are using multiprocessing, you are using the right set of communication protocol between them. Make sure you're maintaining the batch integrity when you're sending the request.

The scoring API was already really good for us, we were able to solve most of the CPU side bottleneck. Then we deploy the system in production and we see the GPU utilization metrics, and the metrics were not good. We were scratching our heads like, what is happening? Then we go profile it, use the PyTorch profile and everything, and then what we see here is there was a lot of idle gaps between the GPU kernel launches. I am going to walk you through this graph here. On the first line we have the tokenizer, as with any LLM you will first have to tokenize it. This is happening on the CPU side. Next comes the scheduler process which is again on the CPU, and this is the process which is preparing the batches to dispatch to the GPU.

According to recent reports, the third line is the GPU compute where you have the kernel releases, all the matrix multiplications happening. In our case, for ranking, we are scoring 50 prompts at the same time. What we were doing in our code was we are copying the yes or no probabilities one by one for each request for each prompt in a synchronized blocking way. This essentially stall the scheduler from launching the next kernel launch for the next request. In order to fix this, we replace this synchronous blocking call into an asynchronous non-blocking copy, and also instead of copying the yes or no probabilities of each and every item, we replace with a batched copy. This helped us to better overlap the CPU work of the previous request while we dispatch the GPU work of the next request. The key takeaway from this slide is if you have Python systems and if you are working with tensors and all sorts of things, just make sure you are using asynchronous non-blocking copies. For example, like when we are using some tensor and copying the tensors from GPU to CPU, a simple dot to list Python call made the copy blocking. All these are subtle things which can affect your overall GPU utilization, and we have not even gotten into kernel yet, everything is happening on the CPU side.

The next thing, once we solved all the CPU side, and all the CPU bottlenecks were handled, we were looking into what work we were doing redundantly and trying to figure out if we can optimize for it. Let's revisit the ranking use case where you have the query and the items. When you are ranking 50 items you are constructing 50 prompts. If you look at the query path, the query path is repeated across all items. We are redoing the query work every time. That is where we researched a bit and trying to see how we can reuse that work, and that is where we come up with an idea to concatenate all the prompts into just one single prompt to the LLM. The blue blocks here denote the query and the green is the first item followed by a delimiter followed by item 2. We just concatenate all of them, and it is just the one single prompt to the LLM.

The key challenge here is, let's say we have a query job 1 and job 2, when the LLM is processing the job 2 and making a decision for it, it should not bring the context of job 1, or else it is going to give you wrong results. That is where we went a little bit into the kernel and then we introduced the custom Item-Aware Attention Mask, inside the flash into the kernel, so that when the LLM sees job 2 it is going to forget about job 1. By doing this optimization we were able to score n items in single pass, and we were able to naturally reuse the query KVs because we only have it once in the prompt.

I know I went a little bit deeper into the kernel and all, but the next few slides will be really interesting because these are something we didn't expect when we deployed in production, and these are brought by Python. We might have a lot of Python code. The first interesting thing that we encountered in production was, we deploy the system, we make it fast enough, and we deploy in the model server. We go see the production metrics, we were seeing spikes every few seconds in P99 latency. Just to reiterate, for search and recommendation, we are operating at a very strict latency. Usually, the P99 has to be less than 500 milliseconds. We go see the graph and we see every few seconds the P99 spikes by 300 milliseconds or so. The reason here turned out to be the Python garbage collector. Before we even got to that, we spent some time, the usual suspects would be like, there was a surge in QPS, or there was one request that had a longer prompt.

These are like user culprits. You go rule them out, and then you have to spend more time debugging what's happening, and the root cause turned out to be the garbage collector. In model server, when you load the model and there are a lot of long-lived Python objects that get created that lives through the lifecycle of the overall process. What was happening is this Python garbage collector was kicking in every few seconds and was scanning each of these objects to figure out which one it should free. This contributed to almost 300-millisecond spike every now and then. In order to fix this what we did was we started the model server. We warmed it up using some warm-up request. Then Python gives you a beautiful API called gc.freeze, which tells the garbage collector, up until this point, all the objects that got created are going to live throughout the life cycle of the model server, just to ignore it.

In a recent development, after this, whatever temporary object that gets created during the request path is the one the garbage collector will be interested in. With this fix we were able to get the P99 in a stable way. The next bottleneck was Python's infamous Global Interpreter Lock, which effectively makes Python bytecode executable by single thread only once at a time. It's different from how Java and C++ and all those things can give you true parallelism when you are working with threads. Python is a different thing all together. In LinkedIn's system, we take the open-source engines we have, and we take the SGLang engine, and then put it behind a gRPC servicer process. The request comes as a gRPC protobuf and the servicer process is the one which is going to deserialize the request. It's also going to do some observability, logging, metrics, and other stuff, and then dispatch the request to the SGLang worker process.

Because of the Global Interpreter Lock, and when we send large QPS the single servicer process became the bottleneck. In order to fix this, we replaced a single process with multiple processes, so that all of them can do this work in parallel in separate CPU cores. Once we solve the bottleneck on a servicer with multiprocessing, the SGLang worker process which is effectively preparing the work and dispatching the work to the GPU became the bottleneck. The fix here is again the same, instead of one process you will have multiple processes. The callout here is, each process has its own model copy and it's going to have its own CUDA stream and do the kernel releases and MemSync and whatnot, and it's effectively going to time slice the GPU. In our case we were able to do it because the model was smaller. Nowadays I think we get enough HBM in the GPU, so you should be able to deploy this as well. The callout again here, in production systems based on Python, is, worry about this Global Interpreter Lock and this can be your single fix which can help improve the throughput.

I know I went a little deeper into the inference side of things. I'm going to keep it really simple in the last four slides. It's pretty simple. These are the major learnings that you could take away from this talk and from our work. The first one is what I call benchmark what you serve. You will be like, "Sundara, that's so obvious. What are you doing otherwise?" I will tell a small story of what we did. We do all these beautiful optimizations in model, context, inference, and then we go and do an offline benchmark. We figure out the throughput we were able to get out of a GPU and then we know how much QPS we want to serve. We do the estimates, and we go inform our leadership, this is the amount of GPUs we need. They were happy and we were happy they were happy.

It has been revealed that we go deploy this in production and we send some dark traffic, that's where we see an entirely different result. We were not able to realize the offline benchmark numbers we were able to get. We are scratching our head like, what is wrong here? Is there anything wrong with the hardware? Is there anything wrong with the specific GPU, or is there any communication bottleneck between the client and server? Something happening over the network. It turned out, we were doing our benchmarks incorrectly. When we are simulating synthetic traffic, we were effectively using even distribution to send the request. What it means is within a second interval, you are estimating based on QPS. You're going to say that my throughput is 1000 jobs per second, 1000 items per second, or something of that sort. When you're simulating the synthetic traffic, the requests are getting sent in an equally spaced manner.

All of them arrive in a uniform distribution with equal spaces. In production, when you're serving real time user traffic, you cannot expect the users to follow the same patterns. Within a second interval, you might have a surge in requests so the queue depth increases. After that, there could be some quieter periods. The major takeaway from this here is if you are serving systems in production, the closest possible result you can get is if you can record and replay your production traffic. If you don't have that option, the second closest thing you could get is if you can simulate the synthetic traffic using a Poisson distribution instead of an even distribution. Just make sure you're doing the right thing there. The second learning is what I call offline must match online. What do we mean by this? When you're working with a model-based system in production, there is an engineer who's going to work on fine-tuning the model.

There'll be prompt engineers who are designing the prompts, and they have their own set of code. The system that gets deployed in production is entirely different. You might be leveraging an open-source system, or you might be leveraging your own model server. There are a set of defaults which is different from both these. Like for example, a simple tokenization config like add end of sequence or beginning of sequence config, can change the entire prompt in itself. You have to make sure there is absolute parity between the offline and the online system. Don't discover all these disparities or discrepancies in production. Disparity has to be a gate without which you cannot launch in production at all.

In a recent development, the third learning is the crux of the talk. There is no single fix here when you are serving systems in production, models, LLMs, anything of that sort. You have to squeeze in throughput from all the possible places. You have to make the model as small as possible, and you have to make the context as short as possible and make the inference as efficient as possible. The final learning, if there are any tech leads, managers, and leaders, this is for you guys. When you are dealing with production systems, there are multiple actors here. You have the inference engineers. You have the model engineers. You have the prompt engineers. You have the product managers who are defining the product policies. It's very crucial that we bring all of these actors into one setup, one meeting which is recurring. You can have a standup or a meeting every week so that each of them can share their idea, cross check, cross validate everything.

In a recent development, you will be surprised how many issues you can catch in these meetings before even you get to production. We often think about optimizations as, if we have to optimize the code, we have to optimize the CPU, GPU, Python, Java, C++, Rust, and all those things. The first and foremost optimization we had to do is with respect to bringing the right people together, you remove the communication barrier and make sure you allow them to share their ideas, and then effectively improve the overall system in play.

Participant 1: Can you tell me more about that single token embedding?

According to recent reports, sundara Raman Ramachandran: The idea here is you can use LLMs as a cross encoder. What it essentially means is you can give full text and then get one single embedding representation out of it. There are multiple techniques how you get this embedding. You can do some last token pooling is what they call. You make the model to do a complete forward pass and then just take the embedding from the last token. We expect the last token to have the complete context of the entire full text. That is one way. The other way is you can take the embedding for each token and then do an average of all these embeddings to get the average template. There are multiple techniques out there. What worked for us is the last token embedding. We take the full text, give it to an LLM, use it as an encoding model, and then get the one single job embedding representation.

Effectively, if you think about it, like from 2000 tokens, this has become one token. In LLM systems internally, this is how it works. You give a list of tokens, let's say 100 tokens. All this first gets converted into one embedding for each of these 100 tokens. The embedding is the input to the overall matrix multiplication that goes into the model. Then it's finally going to spit out another embedding, and then you convert this embedding back, map it to another token, and that becomes your output. Embedding is the one which is the input to the matrix and everything is multiplied between.

Industry observers note that participant 2: You talked about pruning the models themselves, the visible layers that weren't needed. How did you go about identifying the parts that weren't needed and pruning them?

Sundara Raman Ramachandran: The question was more about the structured pruning, how we identified the layers and the MLP layers we have to prune, and what are the techniques we employed.

Sources indicate that this is where it comes in a bit of a trial and error, in a research way. Where we take the model, the 0.6B student ranker which we got, and then we do some SFT based techniques where we mask out certain layers. You start by removing certain MLP layers, one before the last layer, before we prune it, and then do some quality analysis to figure out if the current quality is good enough for the use case. You predict this quality and then you do again a post-training or a pre-training approach to improve the quality again. There is a lot of RL-based fine-tuning you can do further to improve the quality. Those are the techniques we employed.

The question is how much efficiency we were able to save with using the system.

We are optimizing for two things here. One is we want to drive the user engagement. When you think about all the social media websites, we want to make sure two things here, one is the relevance. We want to show the most relevant possible result. If you are searching for someone, the first result has to be the exact person you are searching for. That is number one. The second thing, if you're thinking about job ranking and all, it's really the job engagement which we are looking for. The most vital thing is to improve the product metrics here. We were just comparing with the earlier techniques, what we employed versus this, and how much engagement we are able to improve, how relevant results we are able to give. The throughput on the other things come next for major companies like LinkedIn. Once we make sure we are able to see significant product policy improvement, then we go back and try to optimize on how much throughput we can squeeze.

This is an iterative process. Right now, we are here, we have already optimized good enough, but if you are asking the question about previous retrieval models or previous ranker models, the previous ranker models were just small MLP models where you can just do a couple of multiplication and get the cosine similarity or something. Obviously, that's going to be faster, but is this the thing which is giving you the right answer? No. If as an end user experience, if I give you the wrong answer by doing that, that's not helpful. That's why we compare the product quality and then comes the throughput and cost savings and everything.

Participant 3: What was the product quality difference that you saw between using this LLM based re-ranking versus the previous re-ranking methods?

In a recent development, sundara Raman Ramachandran: I've discussed all this in the blogs, and there are a couple of associated papers also. I think we were able to see, if I'm not wrong, close to like a 5% to 10% increase in the auction metrics, is what we call it, the relevance metrics and all.

Participant 4: It's not related to the ranking, but for the retrieval, how do you handle the security part when you retrieve the information, the compartmentalization of the data?

Sundara Raman Ramachandran: You're asking, when we retrieve the information about the jobs and all, how do we handle the security part of it?

Industry observers note that participant 4: When the user asks a question, how do you make sure to retrieve the results only that the user allowed it to? With all the pruning and all other models, how do you handle this part?

Sundara Raman Ramachandran: Let's look at the job ranking scenario. The job description or job text is posted in public. There is no PII data which is available in the job. All those things get pre-filtered if there is something. For example, when we are working with people search or member profile, we're going to mask all the public information data or the private data, which is not exposed in their LinkedIn profile already. If there is something, for example, the date of birth or something, that's going to get masked out there. It's not even fed into the model at all. Only the publicly available information goes as input to the model.

Participant 5: Since you're saying this is in production, and I believe there's millions of requests every second happening for this kind of request search, I was wondering how this LLM infrastructure integrated with the existing service or server to handle this huge amount of requests?

Sources indicate that sundara Raman Ramachandran: I believe the people search and job search is right now rolled out to all premium consumers. It, I think, gradually will get rolled out to all users by end of this year. In terms of the actual server in production, I show a block diagram in the end. This is what we actually have in production. This is the entire model server high-level architecture. We are using a Python-based gRPC server, and we are leveraging an open-source engine, SGLang. It sits behind the Python gRPC servicer. It's all part of one application per se. It's not split into multiple, I believe. It's not like a multi-servicer and all, it's just one Python application. All these are just Python processes in the end. This is the model server. Essentially, this model server is the one which will fit into the ranker block, which we saw in the architecture diagram. This is the piece which is taking the query and the list of candidates, and it's going to give the scores for each of the candidates.

The Agent Noted It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • In a recent development, figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

In a recent development, figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

In a recent development, two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

Sources indicate that you can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

In a recent development, the gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

Industry observers note that A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

In a recent development, an agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

Sources indicate that we use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Industry observers note that claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

According to recent reports, only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Industry observers note that kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Industry observers note that claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

Recent findings suggest that A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Industry observers note that capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

Industry observers note that we took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

It has been revealed that A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Sources indicate that figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

It has been revealed that the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

It has been revealed that none of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

Recent findings suggest that we assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

Sources indicate that thinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Sources indicate that each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

Sources indicate that at the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

Sources indicate that the trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

According to recent reports, now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

Recent findings suggest that the OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

In a recent development, the useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

Futexes are a kernel subsystem that provides support for fast mutexes in user space. While futexes can indeed be fast, they are not fast enough for a number of users. Partly as a result of that, the implementation of futexes has grown in complexity over the years, with two basic variants on offer. The desire for faster futexes remains, though, and that inspires newly introduced patches, including this series from Suleiman Souhlal adding a third futex class called "futex PING" for "priority inheritance next generation".

The company charges based on usage and sees an opportunity to handle more types of work within each institution. Initial deployments are relatively standardized, while adding workflows requires more engineering with customers. Arva was founded in 2024 by Shah and chief technology officer Oli Wales and operates from London and Newly introduced York. Its research architecture builds specialized reasoning layers on general-purpose language models for tasks such as matching identities, tracing beneficial owners and processing adverse media.

Analyst adjustments, escalations and corrections are anonymized into evaluation datasets. Agents are graded against expert-labelled datasets and adversarial cases before deployment, and subsequent changes are regression-tested against them.

AgentCore, Arva’s continuous-learning system, identifies recurring review patterns and proposes evidence-backed recommendations. It validates changes through historical replay and tracks performance after deployment, while customers decide which recommendations to apply in their own sandboxed environments.

The Series A follows Arva’s January 14, 2025 announcement of a $3 million round led by Gradient, with Y Combinator, Amino Capital, Olive Tree Capital and fintech angels participating. That announcement centered on automating Know Your Business verification, a compliance process for assessing business customers against risks such as fraud and money laundering. The platform turned fragmented registry, website, social-media and document data into business risk assessments.

Industry observers note that an October 2, 2025 case study provides a more specific deployment example. Arva described an unnamed large U.S. bank whose rules-based transaction-monitoring system generated thousands of alerts daily. Arva added a decisioning layer between alert generation and human review rather than replacing the existing system, classifying alerts for automatic resolution, elevation or escalation and producing an audit explanation for each decision.

Industry observers note that arva reported that the deployment reduced alerts sent to human analysts by 78% and eliminated the backlog within 45 days, with a false-negative rate below 1% during a 90-day quality-assurance period. The bank was expanding Arva into adjacent processes, including case-narrative drafting and suspicious activity report enrichment.

According to recent reports, arva’s expansion depends on two connected challenges: winning approval at a relatively small set of large banks, then turning each initial deployment into additional workflows. The planned sales and research spending addresses both, but the organization’s deployment model makes the constraint clear: broader automation has to remain explainable, validated and under customer control.

#23130. Introducing Falcon ASR

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing Falcon ASR

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.
  • Recent findings suggest that we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect.
  • Sources indicate that in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

Recent findings suggest that we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

Sources indicate that in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Industry observers note that arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

Industry observers note that the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

Industry observers note that WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Sources indicate that public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Sources indicate that falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

According to recent reports, the model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Recent findings suggest that falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

Sources indicate that we thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

Industry observers note that يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

Recent findings suggest that درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

Sources indicate that ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:.

Sources indicate that سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

It has been revealed that يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

Industry observers note that يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

Industry observers note that يعكيكم العافية علي المجهود الطيب... بس بغينا نشوف موديلات صوتية STSو TTS بالللهجة الإماراتية لو أمكن.

The announcement comes as franchise dealers rely more heavily on used-vehicle operations as a primary profit center, making pricing, acquisition and inventory decisions central to the software’s business case.

Wavecrest managing partner Deepak Sindwani and principal Anthony Giannobile joined VINCUE’s board concurrently with the financing. They will advise on strategy and operational scale and help facilitate business and technical partnerships across Wavecrest’s portfolio.

Industry observers note that the financing follows VINCUE’s introduction of Protos on October 8, 2026, a ground-up rebuild of its vehicle-lifecycle platform. VINCUE notes Protos Intelligence includes eleven AI agents spanning inventory planning, buying, management and sales, with each agent measuring findings against an individual dealership’s playbook and thresholds rather than generic rules.

Sources indicate that VINCUE claims the system reads more than 2,000 known signals per vehicle identification number, spanning pricing, marketing performance, reconditioning, appraisals and sales activity, and that Signal recommendations are trained on 15 million real sale journeys. A Morning Report ranks vehicles needing attention, lets employees assign actions and add context, and shows the comparisons and reasoning behind recommendations.

The product documentation says pricing checks use recent mileage-matched sales of the same vehicle configuration within 100 miles and flag cases where comparable evidence is thin. Dealers can also type or speak questions to their own inventory data and receive plain-language answers. Signal Appraisal predicts a vehicle’s retail sale price and recalculates the appraisal as managers adjust gross-profit and inventory-turn targets, accounting for holding costs, while the Predictive Market Report forecasts wholesale values rather than reporting past auction results.

Recent findings suggest that VINCUE reported that the first 100 dealers using Buy Center Pro for Service Lane Acquisition and its Benjamin AI agent generated an additional $5 million in front-end gross during the first nine months of 2026. The figure covers service-lane acquisition by that cohort, rather than performance across the broader Protos platform.

The firm also reports more than 20 partner integrations, including Tekion, DriveCentric, LumaScanner, AppraisalPRO and Auto Hauler Exchange. Those integrations place the platform alongside other systems used in dealerships, while VINCUE’s own workflow combines appraisal, acquisition, pricing, stocking and merchandising.

Industry observers note that founded by Chris Hoke, Danny Zaslavsky, Brian Kellogg and Jeff Rice as a mobile appraisal app, VINCUE now covers the vehicle lifecycle from planning and buying through management and sale. The fresh capital extends that evolution through more automated analysis and a larger services organization to help dealers use it.

The financing makes adoption as vital as AI capability. VINCUE’s reported service-lane result covers one product and cohort; the broader test is whether it can produce comparable dealer outcomes across Protos while scaling the support organization that the funding is meant to build.

The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • Industry observers note that over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • In a recent development, the first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Industry observers note that over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern prepares the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

In a recent development, the first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

Sources indicate that A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally states "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub problems made the fallback trainer risky.

Sources indicate that two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

Recent findings suggest that at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

Recent findings suggest that A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

It has been revealed that on the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

Sources indicate that the agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

Industry observers note that ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Recent findings suggest that training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

In a recent development, training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

It has been revealed that I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

Recent findings suggest that ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

Industry observers note that if you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A data center can be full of expensive accelerators and still be short of useful capacity.
  • According to recent reports, in 2027, more of the compute contest will be fought over what each installed system can deliver under the conditions customers actually require.
  • The baseline is already moving quickly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A data center can be full of expensive accelerators and still be short of useful capacity. Some chips are waiting for memory. Others are serving requests that miss their latency target. A benchmark may look excellent while the service bill keeps climbing. Owning the hardware is only the beginning of the economic problem.

According to recent reports, in 2027, more of the compute contest will be fought over what each installed system can deliver under the conditions customers actually require. That shifts attention toward serving software, workload placement and the cost of an acceptable answer.

The baseline is already moving quickly. MLPerf Inference v6.1, released in September 2026, added end-to-end retrieval-augmented generation and an edge agentic workload. It also described the transition toward an API-centric Endpoints suite. This is evidence that benchmark designers are adapting to multi-stage workloads, not evidence that every AI application can be represented by a single benchmark score.

Meanwhile, the IEA’s 2026 energy analysis describes a tension between efficiency gains per task and the growth of more demanding applications. It reports rising data-center electricity use and stresses the uncertainty created by changing workloads. The inference I draw is that falling unit costs will intensify competition over system design while leaving power and memory as consequential constraints. They will not automatically make the total infrastructure bill fall.

The next capacity increase may arrive as a software deployment. Scheduling, memory management and execution kernels can change how much work an installed accelerator completes without changing the chip itself. I expect a reproducible 2027 result showing at least 30% more throughput within the latency target on the fixed hardware and model defined here. The interesting business consequence is additional usable capacity from a purchase the operator has already made.

The economic attraction is straightforward. Hardware that is already installed has a capacity cost whether its scheduler uses it efficiently or not. Better batching, kernel execution, memory allocation, and request routing can raise the amount of useful output without adding accelerators. That is especially valuable where a newly introduced rack would also require more power, cooling, or network capacity.

It has been revealed that the original PagedAttention research demonstrates why memory management belongs in the performance discussion: inefficient handling of the key-value cache can waste capacity and limit batching. Its historical results should not be carried forward as a universal speedup on current systems. They establish the mechanism, rather than the size of the next gain.

Recent findings suggest that there is contemporary evidence of continuing headroom. In its v6.1 submission analysis, AMD reports higher throughput on the same MI355X hardware between benchmark rounds, including a 38% Server improvement on its specified GPT-OSS-120B configuration. That vendor comparison concerns a different model from my forecast target. It supports the proposition that software maturity still matters; it does not establish that a 30% gain on Llama 3.1 8B is guaranteed.

Sources indicate that the fixed workload in this prediction is deliberate. A claim that one system produces more tokens after switching to a smaller model, lower quality, or a looser latency target tells a different economic story. The test needs to hold those choices still. AMD’s published reproduction recipes provide a useful example of exposing software and configuration details, even though vendor-provided recipes still require independent scrutiny.

Look for serving benchmarks that improve throughput on hardware already installed while holding the model, answer quality, and response-time requirements steady. Published configurations and latency distributions will make those gains easier to assess. Results achieved through smaller models, lower precision without quality checks, or relaxed latency targets would support a different claim.

Infrastructure buyers should measure the headroom in their current serving stack before committing to more accelerators. Compare the cost of software upgrades, tuning, and operational support with the capacity they could unlock. Expansion decisions should use accepted requests under the application's service targets, so a higher headline token rate does not conceal a poorer customer experience.

Recent findings suggest that reading a long prompt and generating an answer ask different things of a serving system. Putting both jobs on the same hardware is convenient, but convenience can leave expensive resources poorly matched to the work. In 2027, named operators will show where separating those stages produces a substantial gain in requests served per accelerator-hour. The result will depend on traffic shape; a better architecture for one service can be an unnecessary complication for another.

Sources indicate that prefill processes the incoming context. Decoding generates the answer token by token. Their resource demands and latency objectives differ, which means a shared pool can create interference or force overprovisioning. Splitting the phases allows separate allocation, but adds the cost of moving state between them.

In a recent development, distServe formalized that trade-off around goodput: work completed within the service’s latency constraints. Its reported improvements came from particular evaluated workloads and conditions. They should not be read as a general multiplier for every production cluster. Network topology, context length, output length, and traffic variation determine whether separation pays for itself.

Recent findings suggest that by 2026, this is more than a research proposal. NVIDIA Dynamo includes a planner, cache-aware routing, and transfer components for distributed inference. NVIDIA’s analysis of multimodal disaggregation is useful partly because it identifies conditions where benefits shrink or a topology underperforms. A supplier describing the losing conditions gives buyers a more useful starting point than a single maximum speedup.

My forecast is conditional on the right workloads reaching sufficient scale. Long prompts and uneven demand can create enough scheduling friction to justify a more complex serving architecture. Small, steady workloads may be served more economically by keeping the system simple. Separating stages is therefore a capacity-management decision, with software and operational costs that must be earned back.

Industry observers note that watch for operators publishing results from real request mixes, including long prompts, variable demand, and the cost of moving state between inference stages. Gains should remain visible after all reserved accelerators and transfer overhead are included. Deployments that add complexity without improving useful work per unit of capacity would narrow the case for disaggregation.

Treat prefill–decode separation as an architecture choice to validate against your traffic. Teams should model the extra networking, scheduling, and operating demands before adopting it. Large, uneven workloads may justify that effort; smaller services should require evidence that the additional components earn back their cost under normal operating conditions.

It has been revealed that A cheaper accelerator is a bargain only if the finished answer is acceptable and arrives in time. That leaves room for alternatives to NVIDIA on selected workloads, even while software maturity and availability remain formidable advantages for the incumbent. I expect independent 2027 comparisons to demonstrate a meaningful cost advantage across two different alternative families. The comparison has to survive the migration and operating details that disappear from a chip specification sheet.

This is a prediction about specific operating points, not a prediction of a wholesale platform replacement. A serving stack can be attractive for one model and traffic pattern while being unsuitable for another. Porting effort, operator familiarity, supported kernels, and the availability of useful instances can outweigh a favorable hardware specification.

According to recent reports, several suppliers already offer substantial alternatives. Google’s Ironwood documentation specifies high-bandwidth memory capacity, bandwidth, and interconnect characteristics. AWS’s Trainium3 availability announcement describes a platform designed for dense and expert-parallel workloads. AMD’s MLPerf submissions establish standardized workload participation. None of these sources, by itself, proves the price advantage in my forecast.

The comparison becomes economically meaningful only after the workload is fixed. If an accelerator requires more hosts, a different parallelism scheme, or longer reservation commitments, those costs belong in the denominator. An advertised price that cannot be purchased in the tested region should not determine the result. The same applies to unused reserved capacity and a favorable benchmark assembled from hardware that customers cannot actually obtain.

I assign moderate confidence because technical competitiveness and transparent economics are separate hurdles. The test may be achievable while its cost details remain commercially private. It is also possible for a competing accelerator to win on throughput while losing on operational simplicity. A complete decision should show recurring infrastructure expense and one-time migration effort separately.

According to recent reports, look for comparisons run by organizations other than the winning chip supplier, using purchasable capacity and equivalent quality and latency requirements. The decisive evidence will include host, networking, idle capacity, and migration assumptions. A compelling accelerator specification without a reproducible serving-cost comparison would leave the economic prediction unproven.

Recent findings suggest that build hardware evaluations around a representative model and traffic trace, then price the complete deployment. Keep recurring operating savings separate from porting, retraining staff, and maintaining another software stack. An alternative accelerator can be attractive for a specific service without becoming the right platform for every workload the business runs.

Sources indicate that an agent can consume energy while thinking, calling tools, retrying and eventually failing. Measuring one inference step misses that story. By the end of 2027, I expect the MLPerf lineage of agentic benchmarks to put measured system energy beside successfully completed work. That would give operators a better denominator for a difficult question: how much infrastructure does this service consume to produce something the customer can actually use?

An agent can make repeated model calls, revisit a long context, invoke tools, and retry failed steps. A per-token energy figure captures only part of the cost of that behavior. The relevant unit for a multi-step workload is the completed task, with a declared boundary around the infrastructure being measured.

The v6.1 announcement already describes growing conversational history in agentic inference, an edge agentic test, and work toward datacenter agentic benchmarking. The forecast therefore concerns a further measurement requirement, rather than the debut of agentic benchmarks. I expect pressure to connect those workloads to system energy as inference buyers confront power constraints.

In a recent development, the IEA’s 2026 assessment provides the broader reason to care: the relationship between efficiency and total demand depends on uptake and workload complexity. A short-answer query and a long-running agent cannot be assigned the same representative energy cost. Likewise, an efficient individual accelerator does not establish an efficient complete workflow.

This prediction has the lowest confidence in the article because measurement standards take coordination. Tool services may run outside the measured system. A benchmark may choose reproducibility over realism, or report power without an end-to-end task success gate. Those can be defensible design decisions, but they would not satisfy this particular forecast.

Sources indicate that watch for agentic benchmark reports that put measured energy beside completed tasks and explain which components are inside the measurement boundary. Repeated model calls, retries, and unsuccessful attempts should remain visible. Reporting only accelerator power or energy per token would leave buyers with an incomplete picture of the cost of a multi-step agent.

Capacity and sustainability teams should agree on a useful unit of work before comparing energy figures. Track how many tasks succeed, the resources consumed by failed attempts, and the infrastructure excluded from the estimate. That accounting can help teams decide whether a more capable agent also makes efficient use of their available power and compute budgets.

Industry observers note that the scarce resource will be capacity that meets the service requirement at an acceptable cost. Faster chips will matter, but so will a scheduler that wastes less, a memory layout that fits the workload and a measurement that counts failures honestly. The next data-center advantage may be less visible than a latest rack—and more consequential to the bill.
